condition: when revising a drafted argument section by section

statement: A section with very little evidence may leave its reason unsupported, while a section with abundant evidence but no visible reason may be a data dump.
condition: when auditing the balance between reasons and evidence
exception: the appropriate proportion varies by genre, claim, and section function

statement: Before finalizing an argument, check data and source language against notes and make the relevance of each reported item explicit.
condition: when revising the quality of evidence

statement: Check that no intermediate subreason is missing between evidence and the major reason it is supposed to support.
condition: when evidence appears disconnected from a section point

statement: Revise claims with scope and certainty qualifiers wherever the evidence does not support an unqualified assertion.
condition: when evaluating whether an argument overstates its case

statement: Revise an argument to resemble a hard but collegial conversation by answering the most important skeptical questions and alternatives.
condition: when the draft reads as a contest or ignores competing views

statement: Write down each section's important unstated warrant and state and support it if intended readers are unlikely to accept it.
condition: when auditing inferential completeness
exception: shared, uncontested warrants can remain implicit

statement: Recurring main-point terms and their conceptual relatives should appear through most of the paper so readers can track the central themes.
condition: when revising whole-paper coherence
exception: mechanical repetition should not replace substantive conceptual continuity

statement: A passage that cannot naturally connect to the paper's key concepts may be off track and should be rewritten or removed.
condition: when a passage lacks the conceptual vocabulary linking it to the main point

statement: Mark section boundaries clearly enough that a reader could identify them even when the final genre does not use headings.
condition: when revising macro-organization

statement: Section openings should signal the logical relationship to preceding material, not merely announce a new topic.
condition: when readers need to understand why sections occur in their chosen order

statement: Every section should answer an argument question or perform an identifiable contextual function; otherwise it should be reconsidered or cut.
condition: when auditing how each section serves the whole

statement: State a section's point near the end of its brief introduction or, if necessary, in its conclusion rather than burying it midsection.
condition: when readers need a frame for section-level evidence

statement: Long or fact-dense sections may need a concluding restatement and progress summary to keep the argument visible.
condition: when accumulated detail may obscure the section point
exception: short or conceptually transparent sections may not need a summary

statement: Give each section its own recurring terms that distinguish its contribution from other sections while linking it to the main argument.
condition: when testing section coherence and differentiation
exception: sections with substantially overlapping distinctive terms may need to be combined

statement: Open a paragraph with its key concepts and place its point at the opening or ending rather than in the middle.
condition: when revising paragraph-level guidance for readers
exception: rigidly identical topic-sentence placement can make prose mechanical

statement: A paragraph should be long enough to develop its point but short enough to preserve focus; repeated very short paragraphs may signal underdevelopment and very long ones may signal digression.
condition: when paragraph length affects comprehension
exception: short paragraphs can deliberately emphasize transitions or important statements

statement: Use paragraph breaks as conversational pauses that mark a completed point, allow processing, or signal a transition.
condition: when arranging paragraphs for reader rhythm

statement: After letting a draft rest, skim only its top-level frame and paraphrase the argument to test whether its organization remains intelligible.
condition: when time permits distance before final revision

statement: An outside reader's ability to summarize a skimmed paper predicts how well final readers will grasp its argument.
condition: when the outside reader follows the same high-level reading path

statement: An abstract should identify the research problem, announce key themes, and state the main point or a launching point consistent with field norms.
condition: when the publication genre requires an abstract
exception: some fields or genres do not use abstracts

statement: Choose an abstract pattern by examining representative field journals, deciding whether readers need only the result, a launching preview, or a method-and-evidence summary.
condition: when selecting how much of the argument to compress into an abstract

statement: Put likely search terms in the title and opening of the abstract so later researchers can discover the work.
condition: when research will be indexed or found through keyword search

statement: Build the paper primarily from the researcher's own language and analysis while using source material to support that thinking.
condition: when incorporating prior work into a research paper

statement: Summarize for broad context or low-relevance detail, paraphrase when meaning and detail matter more than wording, and quote when the wording itself serves an essential function.
condition: when deciding how to represent a source and quotation is permitted
exception: source rights or project policy may prohibit quotation even when wording would otherwise be useful

statement: Cite every source-derived summary, paraphrase, and quotation in the field's required style.
condition: when source material appears in the report

statement: Do not stitch copied or lightly transformed source passages together with minimal original prose; synthesize them through the researcher's own argument.
condition: when drafting from electronic notes or downloaded sources

statement: Integrate permitted quotations by identifying, interpreting, or grammatically embedding them rather than leaving them as unexplained insertions.
condition: when direct quotation is allowed and necessary

statement: Any permitted alteration to quoted language must preserve the source's meaning and visibly mark omissions or changes according to field conventions.
condition: when editing a quotation for fit or brevity

statement: Introduce complex evidence with an explicit reason or interpretation showing what readers should infer from it.
condition: when evidence does not transparently express its relevance to the claim

statement: Complete, accurate citations strengthen credibility by letting readers locate sources and audit evidence.
A source list lets readers assess the currency, range, depth, and omissions of a paper's engagement with prior research and extend their own bibliographic search.
condition: when readers inspect citations before, during, or after reading

statement: Citations acknowledge intellectual debts and sustain the reputational exchange on which research communities depend.
Use the citation style required by the field or assignment and verify software-generated citations against the governing guide.
condition: when preparing citations and bibliography

statement: Cite a source whenever using its words, distinctive ideas, or methods unless the information is genuinely common knowledge in the field.
condition: when incorporating another person's intellectual work
exception: widely shared field knowledge not associated with a specific originator generally needs no citation

statement: Mark the boundaries of exact source language even when the source is cited, following the quotation practices of the field.
condition: when reproducing distinctive source wording and quotation is permitted
exception: some fields have special conventions for standard legal or formulaic language

statement: Create a paraphrase from an understood idea without following the source sentence word by word, then compare it against the original for overly parallel wording and order.
condition: when restating source content in original language

statement: Attach citations during drafting as soon as source material is inserted so its provenance is not forgotten or confused with the writer's own work.
condition: when adding quotations, paraphrases, or summaries to a draft

statement: A practical plagiarism test is whether the source's author would recognize the words, ideas, or method as borrowed; if so, acknowledge the source and clearly mark exact language.
condition: when uncertain whether attribution is required

statement: Mark every location where source material is used with a citation that maps unambiguously to the full source entry.
condition: when integrating sources into a paper

statement: An in-text citation should contain only the author, date, title, and location elements required by the chosen style to identify the matching source and passage.
condition: when using a parenthetical citation system
exception: the exact elements vary by style and by whether author information already appears in the sentence

statement: Use notes or parenthetical citations according to field or assignment conventions and consult the current governing guide for exceptional cases.
condition: when selecting and applying a citation system

statement: Present a small, simple set of quantitative values in prose when a graphic would not improve comprehension.
condition: when readers can readily retain and compare the values in a sentence

statement: Use a visual representation when the quantity or relationships among values would be difficult for readers to track in prose.
condition: when the data contain enough values or structure to overload verbal presentation

statement: Choose a graphic form for the truthful rhetorical effect the argument needs rather than using the first available format.
condition: when several graphic forms could display the same data

statement: Use a table when exact discrete values matter and readers can reasonably infer the relationships or trends.
condition: when precision is more important than immediate visual impact
exception: the prose should still identify any relationship readers must not miss

statement: Use a bar chart to emphasize contrasts among discrete categories.
condition: when category comparison is the intended message

statement: Use a line graph when continuous change or a trend over an ordered dimension is the intended message.
condition: when observations form a meaningful sequence such as time

statement: Novices should prefer familiar basic graphics, while advanced researchers should learn the wider visual repertoire expected by their field.
condition: when selecting among visualization techniques of varying complexity
exception: a complex form is justified only when it communicates relationships that simpler forms cannot

statement: Do not let software defaults or decorative capabilities determine a graphic's design; clarity of the argumentative point governs.
condition: when creating graphics with automated tools

statement: Give every graphic a concise, descriptive label that identifies its data and distinguishes it from similar graphics.
condition: when a table or figure appears in a report

statement: A graphic label should describe the data without supplying extraneous background or prejudging what the data imply.
condition: when writing a table title or figure legend

statement: Add derived values, annotations, or visual highlighting inside a graphic when they help readers locate the relationship supporting the argument.
condition: when the key trend or comparison is not immediately visible from raw values
exception: added cues must not distort or conceal the underlying data

statement: Introduce each consequential graphic with a sentence explaining how to interpret it and what relationship readers should examine.
condition: when a graphic serves as evidence for a claim

statement: Keep only data relevant to the current point in the main graphic and move record-only detail to an appropriately labeled appendix.
condition: when extra data would distract from the graphic's purpose

statement: Minimize boxes, backgrounds, grid lines, redundant shading, iconic bars, and decorative dimensions that add clutter or distort perceived values.
condition: when simplifying a table, chart, or graph
exception: light guides or grouping marks may be justified by complex comparisons

statement: Use color only to express a meaningful contrast and only when the expected reproduction medium will preserve that contrast.
condition: when color is considered for data encoding
exception: provide distinctions that remain interpretable without color when grayscale reproduction is possible

statement: Label every table row and column and every graph axis clearly, with intervals and units sufficient to interpret values.
condition: when readers must decode a quantitative display

statement: Label lines and segments directly when possible and display exact values only where those numbers matter to the argument.
condition: when a separate legend or unlabeled shape would increase lookup effort
exception: use a legend when direct labels would make the display unreadable

statement: Order table rows and columns by a principle that reveals the intended pattern rather than defaulting to alphabetical order.
condition: when table sequence affects how quickly readers see the point

statement: Round table values to the precision relevant to the comparison and place totals where readers encounter them after the components.
condition: when exact low-order digits add no informational value

statement: Arrange bars and bar groups in a logical order that makes the visual pattern match the intended comparison.
condition: when bar sequence can clarify or obscure the message

statement: Use stacked bars when comparing wholes is primary, because internal segments without a common baseline are difficult to compare precisely.
condition: when each bar is divided into parts
exception: label and logically order segments if their values also matter

statement: Use grouped bars instead of stacked bars when comparisons among corresponding parts matter as much as comparisons among the wholes.
condition: when readers need a common baseline for component comparisons

statement: Reserve pie charts for rough qualitative impressions of part-to-whole dominance or fragmentation, and prefer bars for quantitative comparison.
condition: when choosing how to show proportions

statement: Choose a truthful variable orientation that makes the intended increase or decrease cognitively direct without changing the underlying data.
condition: when the same trend can be expressed through complementary measures
exception: the chosen framing must not hide a relevant countervailing interpretation

statement: Limit the number of lines in one graph and mark or label important data points so readers can distinguish series and values.
condition: when a line graph risks visual overload
exception: more series are justified only when no simpler display can make the necessary point

statement: Build alternative representations of consequential data and test them with someone unfamiliar with the data for clarity and impact.
condition: when multiple graphic designs seem plausible

statement: A graphic must be accurate and honest as well as visually clear.
condition: when representing evidence visually

statement: Do not truncate or expand a scale in a way that exaggerates or suppresses the substantive contrast.
condition: when selecting an axis range
exception: a nonzero baseline may be used when clearly marked and analytically justified without misleading readers

statement: Do not align independently scaled series so that they visually imply correlation or causation unsupported by the analysis.
condition: when plotting multiple measures with different axes or scales

statement: Avoid chart forms whose stacked or spatial geometry causes readers to misjudge values unrelated to the encoded quantity.
condition: when a display's image can create a false impression of change

statement: Do not make a graphic unnecessarily complex or misleadingly simple; preserve the complexity necessary for an honest point.
condition: when simplifying a visual explanation

statement: State the argumentative point a table or figure supports so readers do not have to infer the intended claim from the image alone.
condition: when a graphic functions as evidence rather than a reference-only record

statement: An effective introduction engages readers with a problem they recognize as needing a solution and sustains attention by promising a credible response.
condition: when writing a final research introduction
exception: surface-level attention devices cannot substitute for a consequential problem

statement: Most research introductions share an underlying sequence of contextual background, a problem statement, and a response despite surface differences among fields.
condition: when the genre uses a problem-driven introduction
exception: not every introduction includes all three elements explicitly

statement: Open an introduction with common ground that establishes a shared, initially stable understanding between writer and readers.
condition: when readers need context before they can recognize the research problem
exception: a familiar and intrinsically motivating problem may permit an immediate problem statement

statement: Use the problem to disrupt the opening common ground by identifying how accepted knowledge is incomplete, mistaken, or unsettled.
condition: when moving from contextual background to the research problem

statement: A stable context can increase a problem's force by showing both the specific defect and how it disturbs a broader understanding readers thought secure.
condition: when the context is genuinely relevant to the destabilizing problem

statement: Supply enough common ground for an interested reader who knows the general field but did not share the writer's local conversation or course.
condition: when deciding how much prior context an introduction needs
exception: expert readers may require less background than general readers

statement: Survey only prior sources whose findings the paper directly modifies, challenges, or extends, adding wider context only when needed to locate the problem.
condition: when building an introduction's literature context

statement: A complete problem statement identifies a condition of incomplete knowledge and the more significant misunderstanding or practical cost that follows from it.
condition: when the problem's consequence is not already obvious to readers

statement: State the consequence as a cost of continued ignorance when motivating the problem and as a benefit of new understanding when intensifying the solution.
condition: when both loss and gain framings are accurate
exception: the choice should follow audience and genre rather than mechanically using both

statement: Even when a broad research problem is familiar, state the particular defect in knowledge that this project will correct.
condition: when readers know the field's larger question but not the project's specific gap

statement: A newly formulated or surprising question requires an explicit account of both the knowledge gap and why resolving it matters.
condition: when readers are unlikely to recognize the problem independently

statement: For applied research, connect the missing knowledge to the tangible harm or decision error it creates.
condition: when a conceptual answer is needed to avoid a practical cost

statement: For pure research, connect the immediate gap to a broader and more important understanding that the answer would enable.
condition: when the research seeks knowledge rather than direct action

statement: Test a problem statement by asking why its stated ignorance matters and checking whether the next sentence supplies a credible consequence.
condition: when revising the link between a condition and its significance

statement: A research problem must be framed as a problem for the intended audience, not only as an investigator's private interest.
condition: when seeking readers' investment in the inquiry
exception: private exploratory research may begin without an external audience but needs one for public reporting

statement: If a well-defined audience still rejects the proposed consequence as unimportant, the project may need a different significance chain or a different audience.
condition: when readers reasonably remain indifferent after the problem is explained

statement: Omit a problem consequence only when intended readers already know it so well that stating it would be redundant or condescending.
condition: when shared field knowledge makes the significance immediate
exception: novice or cross-disciplinary readers may still need the consequence stated

statement: End an introduction by either stating the gist of the solution or promising a specific solution path that the paper will deliver.
condition: after establishing context and problem

statement: A delayed main point needs an outline of the solution or argument plan because a vague topic announcement does not earn readers' trust to continue.
condition: when the full claim will appear only in the conclusion

statement: Set the pace of an introduction according to readers' familiarity with the concepts and problem.
condition: when deciding how much explanation precedes the problem

statement: A rapid opening signals an audience of knowledgeable peers, whereas a slower opening signals readers who need more instruction.
condition: when readers infer the writer's assumptions from introductory pacing

statement: An opening that is too slow for experts can seem elementary, while one that is too fast for novices can seem indifferent to their needs.
condition: when introduction pace mismatches audience knowledge

statement: Treat context, problem, and response as a flexible thinking pattern, omitting an element only when readers already possess it or the chosen structure intentionally delays it.
condition: when organizing a research introduction
exception: the pattern should not be applied as surface formula without audience analysis

statement: Avoid opening by echoing an assignment, invoking a generic dictionary definition, or making an inflated universal claim.
condition: when revising clichéd first sentences
exception: an assignment paraphrase may be used privately to begin drafting but should be replaced

statement: Choose an opening context suited to the specific community of readers rather than one limited to the instructor or broadened to all humanity.
condition: when selecting the introduction's common ground

statement: A striking fact, permitted quotation, or anecdote belongs in an opening only when it anticipates key concepts and directly illuminates the problem.
condition: when using an attention-getting opening
exception: source rights or project policy may prohibit quotation

statement: Begin a conclusion with the main point in a fuller form than its introductory version rather than repeating the same sentence.
condition: when concluding a research argument

statement: Extend a conclusion by stating an additional significance or plausible application that follows from the developed argument.
condition: when the new implication is supported but lies beyond the paper's main analysis
exception: do not introduce an application that the argument makes implausible

statement: A conclusion is an appropriate place to identify new questions enabled by the result and specify research still needed.
condition: when the project reveals consequential unresolved issues

statement: Write the title after the argument is complete and use it to specify the paper's question or claim rather than merely name a broad topic.
condition: when finalizing the paper

statement: Include the main point's key terms in the title so the title, introduction, and body create aligned expectations.
condition: when selecting a final title

statement: Revise sentence style only after the argument and organization are sound, aiming for prose as easy to read as the ideas' real complexity permits.
condition: when beginning a style-focused revision pass
exception: local clarity problems can still be fixed during earlier revision

statement: Dense prose usually reflects insufficient attention to readers rather than irreducible intellectual depth.
condition: for most research writing and most sentences
exception: some genuinely complex reasoning requires more demanding prose

statement: Avoid both opaque academic abstraction and simplistic sentence chopping; aim for the tone of one informed colleague addressing another.
condition: when calibrating research prose for mature clarity

statement: Do not imitate tangled prose merely because it appears in advanced scholarship; disciplinary seriousness does not require unnecessary difficulty.
condition: when learning to write about unfamiliar complex ideas

statement: Apply diagnostic sentence principles during revision rather than constraining exploratory drafting with them.
condition: when using formal clarity techniques

statement: Readers generally find a sentence clearer when its grammatical subject names a main character in the sentence's underlying story.
condition: when revising prose for clarity

statement: Make sentence subjects short, specific, and concrete when the main characters allow it.
condition: when revising sentences for readability
exception: when an abstraction is the most appropriate main character for the intended audience

statement: Express crucial actions as specific verbs rather than as nouns when doing so preserves the intended meaning.
condition: when revising dense or abstract prose
exception: when a nominalized concept is established, useful, and familiar to the intended readers

statement: Turning actions into nouns tends to add articles and prepositional phrases that make a sentence longer and harder to parse.
condition: when verbs or adjectives are nominalized

statement: Nominalizing key actions can force a writer to use vague supporting verbs and can hide or demote the actors responsible for those actions.
condition: when central actions are expressed as abstract nouns

statement: Diagnose sentence clarity by inspecting the opening words of every clause for a concrete subject-character and a verb naming a specific action.
condition: during sentence-level revision

statement: When a sentence fails the character-action test, identify or supply the relevant characters, recover their actions from nouns, and rebuild clauses with those characters as subjects and actions as verbs.
condition: when revision reveals abstract subjects or vague verbs

statement: A usable prose character may be any entity, concrete or abstract, that can serve as the subject of a sequence of actions.
condition: for diagnosing the story implicit in research prose

statement: Prefer concrete entities, especially people, as prose characters when several alternatives would tell the same story equally well.
condition: when choosing among equally suitable focal characters
exception: when an abstract concept better matches the research question or disciplinary audience

statement: Abstract nouns can function clearly as characters when they name concepts already familiar to the intended expert audience.
condition: when writing for readers who share the relevant technical concepts

statement: Treat nominalization as a diagnostic signal rather than an automatic error; retain useful conceptual nouns and revise only those that impede the story.
condition: when reviewing abstract nouns during revision

statement: If an abstraction is the best main character, keep it in subject position but remove surrounding abstractions that the argument does not need.
condition: when the research necessarily tells a story about an abstract concept

statement: Choose the grammatical subject that directs readers toward the character the sentence is actually about, rather than mechanically inserting any available actor.
condition: when multiple implied characters could perform or receive an action

statement: Readers follow a passage more easily when each sentence begins with information made familiar by prior mention or shared context.
condition: when sentences form a connected passage

statement: Begin sentences with familiar information and place new or difficult information near their ends.
condition: when revising a passage for continuity and emphasis

statement: When the character principle conflicts with the familiar-information principle, prioritize familiar information at the beginning of the sentence.
condition: when no revision can satisfy both sentence-opening principles

statement: Diagnose passage flow by checking whether successive sentence openings name a recognizable, related set of familiar concepts or characters.
condition: during paragraph- or passage-level revision

statement: Select active or passive voice according to information flow and story focus, not a blanket rule favoring either form.
condition: when choosing grammatical voice

statement: Passive voice can improve cohesion by moving familiar information into subject position and postponing a new or complex agent.
condition: when the acted-upon entity is familiar and the agent is new, long, or secondary

statement: Avoiding first-person subjects does not by itself make a claim more objective; it changes which character the sentence emphasizes.
condition: when evaluating active and passive formulations in research writing

statement: Use passive voice to describe a reproducible procedure when the actor is interchangeable and the process is the relevant character.
condition: when reporting a process that any qualified researcher could repeat
exception: when the identity or conduct of the actor materially affects the procedure or inference

statement: Use an active first-person construction for interpretations, arguments, discoveries, or other actions for which the authors appropriately claim responsibility.
condition: when the action is specific to the researchers rather than repeatable by anyone

statement: Scientific articles often appropriately use active first person for framing and interpreting the research while using passive voice for generally repeatable procedures.
condition: when the disciplinary convention distinguishes authorial reasoning from replicable process

statement: Introduce an unfamiliar technical term near the end of a sentence so familiar material prepares readers for it.
condition: when a technical term is new to the intended readers

statement: Place long or conceptually complex information at the end of a sentence rather than making readers parse it before reaching the main verb.
condition: when a sentence contains both short familiar material and a complex new unit

statement: Writers can misjudge what is familiar or simple because their own knowledge makes new material feel easier than it will to readers.
condition: when authors assess sentence complexity from their own perspective

statement: End the opening sentence or two of a paragraph with key terms that the following sentences will develop.
condition: when introducing a paragraph or section

statement: Check sentence endings for the information that is newest, most complex, most emphatic, or most important to what follows, and revise when the weight falls elsewhere.
condition: during emphasis and cohesion revision

statement: After revising style for readability, separately check grammar, spelling, punctuation, and field-specific presentation conventions.
condition: during final polishing

statement: Draft enough material to revise before applying detailed sentence diagnostics, because monitoring every stylistic choice during composition can obstruct progress.
condition: during initial drafting

statement: When revision time is limited, first inspect passages whose ideas were difficult to explain, because conceptual difficulty often produces unclear sentences.
condition: when a full sentence-by-sentence review is impractical

statement: Revise clarity and flow in passes: stabilize related sentence openings, align subjects with central characters and verbs with actions, then place familiar information before new information.
condition: when conducting a structured style revision

statement: Nominalization suffixes can help locate candidate abstractions, but the revision decision must depend on whether the noun obscures a needed character or action.
condition: when scanning prose for dense constructions

statement: Do not reject a passive construction solely because it is passive; test whether it improves the sequence of familiar and new information.
condition: when revising a passive sentence

statement: Treat research as a social activity whose ethical effects extend to readers, people affected by its use, and the chain of researchers whose work it incorporates.
condition: when planning, conducting, or reporting research

statement: Evaluate research ethics both by whether conduct sustains a trustworthy community and by whether individual choices honor the principles of that community.
condition: when assessing a research decision

statement: Do not present another person's words, results, or intellectual contribution as your own.
condition: when using or reporting prior work

statement: Do not distort sources, fabricate observations, or falsify results.
condition: when collecting, analyzing, or reporting evidence

statement: Do not report data you distrust without explicitly disclosing the uncertainty about its accuracy.
condition: when evidence may be inaccurate or unreliable
exception: when the limitation is made explicit and the qualified evidence remains useful

statement: Disclose material objections that the argument cannot answer instead of concealing them.
condition: when an unresolved objection could change a reader's judgment

statement: Represent opposing positions in forms their proponents could recognize rather than weakening them through caricature or distortion.
condition: when discussing alternative views

statement: Preserve data and identify sources needed for later researchers to inspect, reproduce, or extend the work.
condition: when records can materially support follow-on research
exception: when lawful confidentiality, safety, or other binding restrictions require controlled access

statement: Ethical research requires positive duties to readers and collaborators, not merely abstention from fraud and theft.
condition: when research is understood as collaborative problem solving

statement: Adopt standards that would sustain a community of shared understanding, rather than standards calibrated only to private advantage.
condition: when setting the quality and honesty threshold for research

statement: Before persuading readers to change their beliefs, consider the responsibilities and foreseeable consequences created if they accept the claim.
condition: when a report asks readers to revise consequential beliefs or actions

statement: Engaging readers' strongest objections respects them as equal participants and tends to improve the reliability of the resulting knowledge.
condition: when alternative views or reservations are relevant

statement: Frame research reporting as a conversation among peers seeking better understanding, even when participants cannot agree on a single common good.
condition: when communicating contested research

statement: Plagiarism harms more than ownership: it denies contributors recognition and erodes the trust on which later research depends.
condition: when unattributed work enters a research community

statement: State conclusions no more strongly than the evidence warrants and identify the limits of certainty.
condition: when reporting a research conclusion

statement: Conducting research develops the ability to read and think critically, including the ability to evaluate research produced by others.
condition: when learners actively perform rather than merely consume research

statement: Teach students to judge their work from the perspective of its readers and of the community whose practices define competent research.
condition: when teaching research planning and reporting

statement: Use the formal features readers expect as tools that guide inquiry and revision, not only as presentation rules applied at the end.
condition: when teaching or performing a research project

statement: Learning how readers interpret reports can improve both writing and the critical reading of other researchers' reports.
condition: when instruction connects reader expectations to author decisions

statement: Do not teach formal research structures as context-free drills, because students may imitate the forms without understanding their purpose.
condition: when introducing inexperienced researchers to report conventions

statement: Connect argument structures to authentic questions so students experience them as aids to inquiry rather than empty templates.
condition: when designing research instruction

statement: Create a rhetorical situation in which student researchers have a recognizable social role, an audience, and meaningful choices.
condition: when constructing a research assignment

statement: Adapt assignment scenarios to the actual students and provide more social and contextual support as their research experience decreases.
condition: when calibrating instruction for a particular class

statement: Define a research assignment around a question or problem to resolve with relevant, reliable evidence, not merely a product to submit for evaluation.
condition: when specifying the desired outcome of student research

statement: Require students to translate private curiosity into a public reason why identifiable readers need the resulting understanding.
condition: when developing the audience and significance of an assignment

statement: Prefer assignments for real readers with a genuine information need; use a well-developed simulation when authentic clients or readers are impractical.
condition: when selecting an audience for student research
exception: when access, safety, time, or scale makes a real audience infeasible

statement: Choose readers whose concerns students can plausibly learn or experience, rather than asking them to invent an unfamiliar professional audience from stereotypes.
condition: when assigning a target audience
exception: when instruction supplies enough access and evidence for students to understand the distant audience

statement: Let a class help define the problems to investigate when classmates will serve as the primary audience, so their interests make peer response substantive.
condition: when turning the class into its own research community

statement: Supply enough real or imagined contextual detail for students to investigate the audience's situation and make rhetorically meaningful choices.
condition: when defining an assignment scenario

statement: Make analysis and discussion of an invented scenario part of the writing process, because no prompt can anticipate every fact students will need.
condition: when a real-world assignment context must be simulated

statement: Build interim reader response into the assignment and direct reviewers to assess substantive argument features rather than merely copyedit.
condition: when staging a student research report

statement: Have interim reviewers respond as the assignment's intended readers and, when useful, divide responsibility among teams reviewing distinct report features.
condition: when organizing peer feedback

statement: Provide a framework of interim deadlines without forcing research through a rigid linear sequence.
condition: when scheduling a research project

statement: Reserve time for false starts, changed questions, revision, and staged criticism because productive research is iterative.
condition: when allocating time for a research assignment

statement: Expect beginners to apply new principles mechanically and treat that awkwardness as a normal learning stage rather than proof of incapacity.
condition: when evaluating novice research behavior

statement: Credit a student who establishes a credible, meaningful problem even if the project does not solve it.
condition: when assessing exploratory or novice research

statement: For an information-gathering project, give the work a public function by positing an intelligent, interested reader who lacks time to conduct the research.
condition: when a course legitimately emphasizes gaining command of a field rather than solving a novel problem

statement: Calibrate research expectations to learners' differing relationships to disciplinary practice, while helping each student recognize and eventually use the core process independently.
condition: when teaching students at different levels of experience and commitment

statement: Treat research design and research writing as coupled activities, because deciding how to explain work often exposes uncertainty about what the work actually establishes.
condition: When planning or describing research

statement: Build technical recommendations and comparisons on robust arguments rather than on an untested preference for one solution.
condition: When proposing an algorithm or explaining why one technical solution is preferable

statement: A technical presentation should communicate a clear message rather than function primarily as a sequence of visually clever slides.
condition: When preparing a spoken technical presentation

statement: Describe algorithms clearly enough that their operation is not obscured by the surrounding presentation.
condition: When communicating algorithmic research

statement: Engage with relevant prior literature even when online access makes it easy to search selectively or stop early.
condition: When positioning new research

statement: Aim for readable, logically organized scientific prose; literary ornament is not required for effective technical communication.
condition: When writing a research paper

statement: Ambiguity, omitted information, and avoidable complexity divert reader effort from understanding the technical content.
A paper that is difficult to understand will struggle to persuade readers even when its results are important and valid.
Strengthen both the supporting argument and its presentation as a result becomes more important, surprising, or initially implausible.
condition: When presenting an important, surprising, or initially implausible result

statement: Structure a submission so reviewers can spend their limited evaluation time on its substance rather than reconstructing the intended argument.
condition: When preparing work for review or examination

statement: A credible paper or thesis should begin from a worthwhile question, use a sound method, and report results clearly enough to persuade a skeptical reader that they are robust and interesting.
condition: When planning and reporting scientific work

statement: Novice researchers can improve an initial paper by imposing a logical organization, writing concise sentences, checking for recurring defects, and soliciting feedback.
condition: When a writer lacks extensive research-writing experience

statement: Use standard research and writing templates as scaffolding for a first competent outcome, then improve beyond them through practice, reflection, and feedback.
condition: When learning research or technical writing

statement: Match the level of detail, evidentiary burden, and claims to the publication form rather than treating books, theses, journal papers, conference papers, and extended abstracts as interchangeable.
condition: When selecting or writing for a publication venue

statement: An extended abstract that omits methodological and evidentiary detail may summarize results without being able to sustain a complete argument for its claims.
condition: When the publication format requires substantial detail to be omitted

statement: Defend and justify the substantive content of a research paper rather than relying on the latitude for opinion sometimes available in books.
condition: When reporting new research in a paper

statement: Organize a research paper around a central hypothesis and include the arguments, evidence, experiments, proofs, and background needed to explain and support it.
condition: When the work can be expressed around a central hypothesis

statement: Exclude routine failed attempts, discarded hypotheses, misconceptions, and experimental mistakes from the final research paper.
condition: When selecting material for a conventional research paper
exception: Include a failure when it is genuinely illuminating; a reflective thesis may justify somewhat broader process discussion

statement: Use writing during research to make ideas concrete, reveal new questions, support systematic discussion, and test whether complex reasoning is robust.
condition: Throughout the development of a research project

statement: Treat substantive writing as part of the research process; only final stylistic polishing is properly deferred until after the research is complete.
condition: When scheduling research and writing work

statement: Writing instruction for novice researchers should extend beyond reactive comments on drafts and include guided practice with experienced researchers.
condition: When supervising researchers who are learning to write extended technical documents

statement: Accept scientific claims provisionally when reasonable evidence supports them and they do not conflict with other provisionally accepted knowledge.
condition: When evaluating a scientific claim
exception: Suspend judgment when decisive information is unavailable; absolute doubt is not a workable default

statement: Design a research program to gather the evidence needed to persuade a reasonable skeptic, without substituting rhetoric or authority for demonstration.
condition: When choosing research questions, methods, and evidence

statement: Explain new ideas clearly enough that other researchers can understand, evaluate, remember, and apply them.
condition: When communicating a new scientific idea

statement: Adapt general writing guidance to the conventions and technical needs of the specific discipline instead of assuming that broad science-writing advice transfers unchanged.
condition: When applying cross-disciplinary writing advice

statement: Develop research and writing competence through repeated practice in collaboration with experienced researchers; reading guidance alone is insufficient.
condition: When training a novice researcher

statement: Treat style guidance as reasoned defaults rather than rigid law, and depart from a convention only for a defensible purpose.
condition: When a writing convention appears unsuitable for the current text
exception: A justified contextual choice can override the default convention

statement: Use writing and research guidance as a browsable diagnostic reference, including checklists during active work, rather than trying to memorize it.
condition: When learning or revising technical work

statement: Consult current specialist resources for methods, ethics, and language challenges when an introductory treatment does not provide enough depth.
condition: When the available guidance only introduces a consequential topic

statement: Build a research project by forming a precise question, acquiring a critical understanding of prior work, gathering relevant evidence, connecting question and evidence through reasoning, and publishing the resulting account.
condition: When organizing an end-to-end research project

statement: Do not substitute software development, essay assembly, user documentation, or coursework habits for the distinct goals and evidentiary standards of research.
condition: When a newcomer is deciding how to conduct or report computer-science research

statement: Judge research value partly by whether others adopt its knowledge or change their practice or understanding; publication is an intermediate step, not the ultimate objective.
condition: When assessing the intended impact of research

statement: Use curiosity and informed conjecture to select an initial direction while acknowledging that novelty, feasibility, and value cannot yet be known.
condition: At the earliest stage of an exploratory research project

statement: Define both the broad problem and the specific initial activities and outcomes before a research program proceeds in earnest.
condition: At the start of a research program

statement: Set clear short-term goals that produce usable outcomes while training the component skills needed for a longer research program.
condition: When a student project also serves as research training

statement: Develop a topic around a strong motivating example so the research remains focused on a useful and assessable outcome.
condition: When converting a broad topic into a research question

statement: Prefer a tractable surrogate question when the ideal real-world problem cannot be investigated with available methods or resources.
condition: When direct study of the desired problem is infeasible
exception: The surrogate must still bear meaningfully on the underlying goal

statement: Evaluate an advisor for working compatibility and the likely durability of the relationship, not only for prestige or topic appeal.
condition: When a student chooses a research advisor

statement: Do not choose a research topic primarily because it is fashionable; require confidence that it will remain relevant over the project horizon.
condition: When a topic is attractive mainly because of a current trend
exception: A trend representing a durable shift can remain a valid consideration

statement: Match a project's technical demands to the researcher's existing abilities and strengths.
condition: When selecting among possible research projects
exception: A training goal may justify some deliberate skill stretch if support and time make it feasible

statement: Assess a field's barrier to entry, including prerequisite knowledge, infrastructure, cost, local expertise, and codebase familiarity, before committing to a project.
condition: When testing the feasibility of a proposed research direction

statement: Consider less mature directions when a popular, well-developed field demands extensive background, offers few open questions, and has unusually strong baselines.
condition: When a mature field's barrier to meaningful contribution is high
exception: Remain in the mature field when the researcher has a credible route past those barriers

statement: For novice research, pursue the smallest question that is still interesting and extend it only after clearly achievable outcomes have been secured.
condition: When scoping a training project or an initial investigation

statement: A project needs enough challenge and uncertainty to permit non-obvious discovery; a merely obvious, trivial increment is unlikely to warrant research.
condition: When judging whether an incremental proposal is research-worthy

statement: A problem with an existing commercial solution can still support valuable research when the work independently measures solution quality or tests unverified claims.
condition: When a production implementation appears to have solved the target problem
exception: The research must yield knowledge beyond reproducing a merely workable implementation

statement: Create a sequence of meaningful deadlines and milestones rather than managing a research project against only its final completion date.
condition: When planning a substantial research project

statement: Implement only the system components needed to investigate the research questions instead of completing a production-scale system by default.
condition: When implementation supports an experimental research question
exception: A complete system is justified when the research question itself requires system-level behavior

statement: Plan backward from the final paper, thesis, or report and treat completion of each required substantive section as a project milestone.
condition: When defining project milestones

statement: Design experiments by predicting how observations should differ if the hypothesis is true versus false, then scrutinize whether the data, code, and platform can produce credible evidence.
condition: When experimental evidence will test a hypothesis

statement: Determine participant selection and ethics-clearance requirements before conducting a study involving people.
condition: When research may involve human participants

statement: Identify project components in advance without assuming they must be completed sequentially.
condition: When scheduling interdependent research activities
exception: A genuine dependency may still require one component to precede another

statement: Begin reading, implementation, analysis, experimentation, and writing as early as dependencies permit, allowing these activities to overlap.
condition: When planning research stages that are often treated as sequential
exception: Do not begin an activity before its indispensable inputs exist

statement: Draft the thesis when uncertainty remains about whether enough research has been done, because a near-complete account makes any remaining evidence gap more specific.
condition: In the later stages of a doctoral project when sufficiency is unclear

statement: Revise day-to-day research priorities as bottlenecks emerge, including pruning goals or allocating more time to writing, while preserving the project's overall aims.
condition: When actual progress diverges from a long-term schedule

statement: Treat a degree research program primarily as supervised training in conducting a project from conception through write-up; publishable work is an expected benefit, not the sole purpose.
condition: When defining the purpose and success criteria of a student research program

statement: Reduce task-level direction as a research student becomes able to anticipate, choose, and own the next steps, shifting supervision from management toward guidance.
condition: As a student demonstrates growing research competence

statement: Calibrate student autonomy to the individual's maturity, support network, and need for assistance rather than applying one advising style uniformly.
condition: When deciding how closely to direct a research student

statement: Scope a student project so it is distinct yet connected to the group's work, open to innovation yet likely to succeed, and close enough to the advisor's expertise for novelty and literature coverage to be checked.
condition: When an advisor and student define a research project

statement: Do not proceed with a student topic merely because one party finds it interesting; confirm that competent supervision is available.
condition: When either the advisor or student proposes a topic outside established expertise

statement: Prepare for advising meetings with concrete results, questions, and an honest account of progress.
condition: Before a student-advisor meeting

statement: Make potential conflicts between joint publication work and thesis progress explicit so student and advisor can agree on priorities.
condition: When co-authored paper work competes with a student's degree milestones

statement: Successful research students tend to read beyond their immediate topic, try ideas, and participate in the wider academic community.
condition: In the author's observations of research training

statement: Develop independence by taking initiative over both the research work and how it is presented, progressively assuming responsibility for the whole project.
condition: As a research student gains experience

statement: Use systematic organization, rigorous standards, and deliberate reflection on working habits to close skill and knowledge gaps.
condition: When developing as an independent researcher

statement: Persistence and resilience after substantial failed work can matter more to doctoral success than exceptional intellectual flair alone.
condition: When assessing readiness for extended research

statement: Before starting, document the research question, project scale, respective student and advisor contributions, required resources, likely obstacles, milestones, and working arrangements.
condition: When establishing a student research project

statement: Read a paper to identify its contribution and value, detect its flaws, and judge whether those flaws materially weaken the work.
condition: When critically reading research literature

statement: Apply the same care, effort, and ethical standards to peer review that are expected in conducting original research.
condition: When reviewing a paper or examining a thesis

statement: By project completion, identify, read, and understand all scientific literature with a significant connection to the work.
condition: Before claiming novelty or submitting the completed research

statement: Ground a research write-up's arguments primarily in reputable refereed papers, examined theses, and authoritative scholarly books; use informal sources mainly to locate such work.
condition: When choosing evidence and citations for a scientific argument
exception: A primary or informal source may be appropriate when it is itself the object of analysis or uniquely documents the relevant fact

statement: Triage a paper by skimming for relevance before investing in a close reading, then allocate deep attention only where the expected value warrants it.
condition: On first encountering a potentially relevant paper

statement: Use distinct reading modes for discovery, general background, and close analysis, and keep reading embedded in a productive research cycle rather than allowing it to become avoidance.
condition: When managing a large research literature

statement: Read the original paper before discussing or citing it; another author's summary is not an adequate substitute.
condition: When a paper will be cited or substantively characterized
exception: Clearly identified secondary synthesis can be cited for its own interpretation

statement: Search literature through multiple complementary paths, including varied terminology, academic indexes, research-group sites, reference chains, recent venues, archives, library browsing, and conversations with researchers.
condition: When seeking comprehensive coverage of related work

statement: Use each search result to refine terminology, identify influential work, discover new search paths, and sharpen inclusion criteria.
condition: During iterative literature discovery

statement: Prefer the version of a paper that its authors treat as definitive, typically the most fully revised published version.
condition: When preprint, conference, and journal versions coexist
exception: Use an earlier version when it contains uniquely relevant material and identify the version precisely

statement: Define relevance broadly enough to include benchmarks, transferable proof techniques, literature insights, and evidence against pursuing a direction, not only competing methods.
condition: When screening literature for relevance to a project

statement: Repeat and revise literature searches as the research question and the researcher's understanding evolve.
condition: Throughout an evolving research project

statement: Separate broad collection from critical evaluation: gather candidate papers during focused search sessions, then analyze and categorize them afterward.
condition: When an exploratory search produces many leads
exception: A quick relevance check is still needed to decide what to retain

statement: If prior work has already solved the original problem, reassess which aspects remain novel rather than concealing the overlap or assuming no further contribution is possible.
condition: When literature discovery undermines the claimed originality of a project

statement: Treat peer review and venue reputation as evidence of research quality, not as guarantees that a paper is correct, relevant, or methodologically sound.
condition: When deciding how much to trust published work

statement: Evaluate research with balanced skepticism rather than classifying papers as wholly sound or wholly worthless; identify which components remain useful and which are questionable.
condition: When a paper contains both strengths and defects

statement: Interrogate each important paper for contribution, correctness, literature coverage, methodological fit, alternative interpretations, technical consistency, and reproducibility.
condition: When performing a close critical reading

statement: Record a reasoned analysis of each important paper and continue revising that analysis as the researcher's own work supplies a more mature perspective.
condition: When a paper may affect later research or writing

statement: Construct a literature review as a topic-organized critical synthesis of contributions, limitations, relationships, and open questions rather than as a sequence of paper summaries.
condition: When writing a literature review

statement: Develop the literature review from the start of reading, capturing bibliographic data, copies, contribution summaries, evidence, shortcomings, and relationships as work proceeds.
condition: Throughout a research project that will require a literature review

statement: Keep early literature-review drafts inclusive and preserve removed discussions in an archive so earlier reading is not lost when relevance judgments change.
condition: During early and middle review drafting

statement: Authors retain responsibility for a paper's correctness, presentation quality, and originality; editorial and peer review do not transfer that responsibility.
condition: When preparing and submitting research

statement: A referee should be objective, fair, confidential, prompt, explicit about limitations and conflicts, and sufficiently careful to recommend acceptance only when the work meets the relevant standard.
condition: When serving as a paper referee or thesis examiner

statement: Do not infer a submission's correctness or significance from polished prose, impressive mathematics, or author prestige.
condition: When reviewing research

statement: Evaluate a paper's contribution through both originality—whether its ideas are significant, new, and interesting—and validity—whether those ideas have been shown to be sound.
condition: When making a publication decision or assessing research quality

statement: Judge a contribution's significance by the changes in practice, understanding, or follow-on research that would plausibly result if the work were widely read.
condition: When distinguishing a minor contribution from a major one

statement: Do not treat an idea's apparent obviousness after it has been clearly explained as evidence that it lacked originality.
condition: When novelty is challenged because a result seems obvious in retrospect

statement: Recognize asking the right question, reorganizing known ideas into a useful framework, or rigorously reevaluating an existing method as potentially original contributions.
condition: When assessing forms of originality beyond a wholly new technique
exception: The new framing or reevaluation must add significant insight or utility

statement: Do not regard intuition alone as a demonstration of validity; provide a correctness argument that other scientists can inspect and verify.
condition: When a paper proposes that an idea or method is sound

statement: Where feasible, demonstrate validity through complementary methods such as proof, analysis, modelling, simulation, or experiment, together with comparison to existing approaches.
condition: When multiple forms of validation bear on the same research claim
exception: The appropriate methods depend on the nature of the claim

statement: Make demonstrations of validity carefully described, thorough, and reproducible, using credible implementations, adequate samples, and appropriate controls where those elements apply.
condition: When reporting a theoretical or experimental validation
exception: Specific design requirements vary with the validation method

statement: Compare a new algorithm with credible existing alternatives; a method shown to be inferior without compensating benefits is unlikely to be a significant contribution.
condition: When evaluating the practical significance of a proposed algorithm
exception: A weaker primary metric may be justified by a distinct benefit or a new explanatory result

statement: Review a submission for timeliness, audience and venue fit, readability, completeness, unnecessary material, and whether its length is justified in addition to technical correctness.
condition: When assessing a paper for a particular publication venue

statement: Require authors to identify their work's strengths, weaknesses, and implications honestly; balanced analysis makes results more credible than ignoring known shortcomings.
condition: When presenting or reviewing a research contribution

statement: Identify the paper's explicit or implicit hypothesis, then use it to test whether all included material is pertinent and whether essential support is missing.
condition: When analyzing the coherence and completeness of a paper
exception: Some descriptive or exploratory papers may organize around a question rather than a single hypothesis

statement: Use a bibliography as a diagnostic signal for scholarship—checking recency, major venues, related work, and self-citation patterns—without treating reference count as a decisive metric.
condition: When evaluating whether an author has established novelty and literature coverage
exception: Some narrowly defined problems genuinely have little prior literature

statement: A submission that omits basic literature search, complete arguments, proofreading, or substantive validation may not warrant a full detailed review.
condition: When a paper is seriously incomplete at a foundational level
exception: Do not classify a paper as foundationally incomplete without enough inspection to justify that judgment

statement: Treat pervasive notation, formula, bibliography, or consistency errors as possible evidence that the underlying results were not checked with adequate care.
condition: When errors form a pattern rather than isolated typographical slips
exception: A small number of harmless typographical errors does not by itself invalidate the research

statement: Readable presentation is necessary for a useful paper but cannot compensate for absent originality or invalid results.
condition: When weighing presentation against substantive contribution

statement: Recommend major revision only when a reasonable amount of additional work could make the current paper acceptable; require a new submission when substantial research and rewriting are needed.
condition: When choosing between major revision and rejection

statement: Declare limitations in subject or proof expertise and do not recommend acceptance when an essential aspect of the paper remains unevaluated.
condition: When refereeing outside complete personal expertise
exception: An editor may combine complementary reviews, but each referee must state what they could not assess

statement: Write a review both to support an editorial decision and to transfer useful expertise to the authors.
condition: When reviewing a research submission

statement: Make the review's case for acceptance or rejection explicit, evidence-based, and detailed enough to persuade the editor; a summary or unsupported verdict is insufficient.
condition: When drafting reviewer comments

statement: Support a claim that work is unoriginal with specific prior references and an explanation of the overlap.
condition: When rejecting or criticizing a paper for lack of novelty

statement: Give authors actionable guidance: specify residual fixes for accepted work, or identify the worthwhile core and a plausible improvement path for rejected work.
condition: When a reviewed paper has remediable defects
exception: If no worthwhile core can be identified, explain the basis for that conclusion rather than inventing a path forward

statement: A superficial review externalizes unresolved defects to later referees and weakens the community's confidence in published work.

Before recommending acceptance, inspect mathematical reasoning, experimental plausibility, bibliography, claim strength, omissions, and irrelevant material because later production checks will not reliably catch substantive defects.
condition: When the reviewer may be the final subject-matter expert to inspect a paper

statement: Scale fine-grained checking down when gross defects already require rejection, but check enough to prevent repeated cycles of piecemeal correction and do not complete the research for the author.
condition: When a paper clearly requires rejection or substantial revision
exception: Suggest simple changes that materially improve otherwise worthwhile work

statement: Keep the publication judgment provisional while drafting the review, because articulating the evidence can reveal either deeper defects or greater significance.
condition: Until the review's reasoning has been fully written and checked

statement: Identify a paper's strengths as well as its defects so authors know which material should anchor any revision.
condition: When writing constructive reviewer feedback

statement: Make criticisms relevant, specific, exemplified where useful, and polite; omit generic complaints that cannot be tied to an actual defect.
condition: When expressing negative findings in a review

statement: Do not place new substantive criticisms only in confidential comments, because authors cannot answer or correct claims they cannot see.
condition: When a review process permits confidential remarks to the editor
exception: Confidential space can communicate the recommendation, emphasize visible points, or disclose reviewer limitations

statement: Organize a research program around a definite hypothesis or research question that determines what phenomenon to observe and what evidence to collect.
condition: When pursuing research intended to produce robust explanatory or predictive outcomes
exception: Some exploratory work may first generate observations from which a later hypothesis is formed

statement: State a hypothesis specifically and unambiguously, including the boundaries of what is not being claimed.
condition: When converting an informal belief into a testable research claim

statement: Qualify a hypothesis with the application, data, operating conditions, and assumptions that delimit its reach; explicit limitations make the claim more precise rather than inherently weaker.
condition: When a universal form of the hypothesis exceeds what can be established

statement: Require a hypothesis to cover a feasibly investigable domain and to admit observations that could show it false.
condition: Before designing a test of a hypothesis

statement: Reconsider whether a research question is worthwhile if making its hypothesis testable requires contrived restrictions or assumes resolution of currently insoluble prerequisites.
condition: When refining an initially vague or overly broad hypothesis
exception: A restricted result may still matter when the restricted domain has independent practical or theoretical importance

statement: Do not treat a black-box algorithm beating a weak baseline on one data set as a strong contribution unless the work yields insight or supports predictions beyond that observed case.
condition: When evaluating empirical application of a poorly understood method
exception: A single-case observation can be valuable when the case itself is consequential and the claim remains explicitly local

statement: Renaming an existing method with fashionable terminology does not create novelty; demonstrate behavior or issues specific to the newly claimed domain.
condition: When repositioning existing work in a new research area

statement: Form the hypothesis before its confirmatory test and, where possible, keep testing blind to tuning data; a hypothesis fitted to the same observations has not been independently confirmed.
condition: When claiming that experimental results confirm a hypothesis
exception: Observations may generate or refine a hypothesis, but they should be distinguished from later confirmatory evidence

statement: Prefer the simpler of two hypotheses when both explain the observations equally well.
condition: When competing hypotheses have equal empirical fit
exception: Additional complexity may be justified by explanatory, predictive, or mechanistic benefits not captured by the fit comparison

statement: Explicitly connect evidence to the hypothesis with reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the stated conclusion.
condition: When presenting evidence for a research claim

statement: Develop an argument by raising likely skeptical objections, answering those that can be rebutted, conceding valid limitations, and disclosing uncertainty.
condition: When constructing the case for a hypothesis

statement: Actively search for counterexamples and include reasoning that resolves objections a careful reader is likely to raise independently.
condition: Before finalizing a research argument

statement: Do not hide an objection that cannot be refuted; disclose it and reassess whether it changes the results or conclusion.
condition: When a material counterargument survives analysis

statement: Pre-screen a hypothesis by testing whether it implies implausible consequences, unfairly requires all earlier researchers to have been foolish, or fails to explain observations covered by the current account.
condition: Before investing heavily in formal or experimental testing
exception: A surprising implication is not fatal when independent evidence makes it credible

statement: Persist long enough to establish whether a doubtful hypothesis remains plausible, but abandon or reformulate it when evidence indicates it is false.
condition: When tests repeatedly challenge a favored hypothesis
exception: Initial contradictory evidence may justify further checking before abandonment

statement: Increase the rigor of attempts to disprove a hypothesis as the researcher's intuitive attachment to it grows.
condition: When confirmation bias is likely because a hypothesis is strongly preferred

statement: Support claims that an algorithm is new, sensible, and effective with a careful literature review, a clear account of limitations, credible code, appropriate data, and enough testing.
condition: When presenting a novel algorithm
exception: The precise evidence depends on whether the contribution is theoretical, empirical, or both

statement: Use objective evidence and supporting explanation to enable skeptical readers to make informed judgments rather than merely asking them to share the author's conclusion.
condition: When writing a scientific case

statement: Treat a formal proof as inspectable evidence rather than infallible truth, while still considering formal analysis whenever the hypothesis permits it.
condition: When selecting or evaluating proof as evidence
exception: Some real-world or highly complex hypotheses are not tractable through formal analysis alone

statement: Do not assume asymptotic analysis alone establishes practical behavior; add evidence suited to real-world effects when those effects matter to the claim.
condition: When a claim concerns practical performance or behavior
exception: Asymptotic analysis can be sufficient when the claim is explicitly limited to asymptotic properties

statement: When using a mathematical model, demonstrate its correspondence to the target phenomenon and evaluate whether simplifying assumptions and tunable parameters make it unrealistically indirect.
condition: When a model supplies evidence about a hypothesis

statement: Use simulation to vary inputs and isolate behavior across controlled ranges, but test whether the simulated properties correspond to reality before generalizing the results.
condition: When real data or full implementation cannot expose the needed range of conditions
exception: A conclusion may remain explicitly limited to the simulated system without real-world validation

statement: An experiment using a full implementation and real or highly realistic data directly tests a hypothesis but, by itself, establishes behavior only for the tested setting.
condition: When interpreting experimental evidence
exception: Careful sampling, modelling, and replication can support broader generalization

statement: Design experiments around prior model-based predictions and choose severe tests, including extremes, that are likely to fail when the hypothesis is false.
condition: When confirmatory experiments can be designed from an explanatory model

statement: Use proof, models, simulations, and experiments to cross-check one another, but label each form accurately and do not claim that one establishes properties it never tested.
condition: When combining multiple forms of evidence

statement: Executing code that merely computes a mathematical model's predictions is not an experiment on the modeled algorithm and does not validate the model's correspondence to that algorithm.
condition: When a program only instantiates equations from a model

statement: Choose the form of evidence that will most convincingly address reasonable skepticism, not simply the form that minimizes researcher effort.
condition: When selecting among feasible validation methods

statement: Prioritize completing a coherent, well-supported write-up over last-minute experiments or superficial literature additions that cannot be integrated responsibly.
condition: When limited time remains before submission
exception: A missing test that determines the validity of the central claim may require delaying submission instead

statement: Expect new, unreviewed work to bear a substantial evidentiary burden because readers reasonably place more trust in already scrutinized knowledge.
condition: When making claims that challenge or extend published findings
exception: Prior publication is itself not proof of correctness

statement: Select measurements that are observable consequences of the phenomenon described by the research hypothesis.
condition: When designing an experiment

statement: Define both what will be measured and the measurement mechanism while developing the research question, and disclose the mechanism's flaws and limitations.
condition: When a research question depends on quantitative or qualitative observations
exception: An exploratory study may refine measures iteratively, but later claims must reflect that history

statement: Verify that each quantitative measure is logically connected to the qualitative research aim rather than assuming that an easy-to-compute proxy captures the intended outcome.
condition: When operationalizing a qualitative goal

statement: Preserve the distinction between the practical goal and its quantitative approximations, using multiple measures when one proxy would encourage optimization away from the real objective.
condition: When no single metric fully represents the desired system quality
