Cut empty amplifiers such as dramatically, very, quite, substantially, and highly, because they take up space without adding meaning and the important thought remains when you delete them; give a concrete magnitude instead, such as increased by a factor of 42.
Watch that modifiers do not hide empty thoughts: when stripping the modifiers leaves little substance, replace the hype with concrete content rather than decoration.

Do not use adjectives that appear to describe the nature of a change but actually cover all possibilities, such as structural and functional changes, because they add no concrete information; state the specific change instead.
Keep modifiers that clarify or define their referent rather than merely amplify it, because a modifier that alters meaning is powerful, so preliminary result cannot be deleted while final result can.

Cut unnecessary metadiscourse such as we found that or in this study we measured, because data first reported in your paper is obviously yours and from this study; keep only the metadiscourse that develops the argument's flow.

Cut verbosity, the rambling that comes from insecurity or from failing to separate your mental process from the story, and pack extra detail into a sentence only when that detail genuinely warrants the space.
Put the action into verbs to condense, because passives, fuzzy verbs, and nominalizations all require extra words.
When text is long, wordy, and confusing at once, first strip away the excess to see what it actually says and then sharpen it, because clutter can bury the message.
Aim for a healthy verb-to-word ratio and active voice with a real actor in the topic position, because depersonalized, nominalized text is both longer and more confusing.

Allow yourself to be a little verbose in first drafts, especially with coauthors, because stripping down overloaded writing is easy while filling the gaps in cryptic, underloaded writing is hard and requires knowing the story well.
condition: in a first draft, especially one that coauthors will help revise

statement: Treat words that build flow and coherence as necessary, because any word that helps readers understand your message does useful work; aim for the golden balance between bloated and cryptic.
Merge the best parts of several weak sentences into one strong sentence rather than trimming each in isolation, taking the stronger concept from one and the stronger core message from another.

Expect writing problems to come in convoluted mixes rather than one at a time, such as broken arcs with weak linkages, prepositional phrases with passives, and jargon with nominalizations, so fix them in multiple passes, each solving one or two and often unmasking others.

Edit top-down in the SCFL sequence (Structure to get the story's OCAR elements right, Clarity to make ideas clear and concrete, Flow to link one thought to the next, and Language to make it sound good), starting with big structural issues before fine details of word use.

Expect the SCFL passes to overlap and to be repeated several times, because solving one problem usually requires considering the others: an unclear topic makes structure hard to define, and clarifying language can force you to rethink the structure of your arguments.

When a sentence's point is unclear because of a buried passive verb, rewrite it into the active voice and decide which story it tells, for example the history of the science versus the biology, because that choice defines the paper's direction.
Read your writing aloud as a final revision step, because your eyes skip over awkward expressions, breaks in flow, and clunky words but your ears catch them.
Package a sentence into compact arcs that each carry a distinct OCAR function, because getting the structure right even within a single sentence solves many problems.
Achieve clarity and grace by sharpening up rather than dumbing down, so you can lose words while keeping professionalism.
After fixing sentences, cycle back to structure, because a passive or pawn-push opening sentence may be worth deleting entirely so you can launch a queen.

Expect to make multiple editing passes that fix one set of problems and expose another, and re-edit repeatedly, because each fresh look and each aloud reading reveals what did not work, which is why editors legitimately re-edit their own edits.

Address limitations with a but-yes structure rather than yes-but: deal with the limitations as early as possible, constrain your conclusions to fit within them, and end on the affirmative, because yes-but makes the limitation the resolution and the most powerful message.

Air limitations up front rather than as fine print, because doing so is more honest, is easier for readers to follow since they never have to back up and reprocess, and lets them work through the data in light of the limits.

Recognize that many apparent limitations come from a mismatch between the question and the methods rather than the methods themselves, and fix them by framing the knowledge gap you can actually fill, sometimes revising the question to match what the method measures.
Address a methodological limitation immediately where you describe the method to lay concerns to rest, because an unaddressed concern makes readers stop reading, get distracted, or stay skeptical.
Address a limitation unapologetically by explaining why the constraint was unavoidable, grounding it in the larger context, and showing how you dealt with it, then not raising it again.

In a proposal especially, disclose and defend methodological constraints and explain why your methods answer your questions, because reviewers will find hidden negatives anyway and reject, whereas open discussion may earn the benefit of the doubt.
condition: when writing a proposal for a critical audience

statement: Treat every method as good when done well, because bad is a matter of interpretation (a method may be bad for measuring one thing but good for a slightly different thing), so explain why your methods give the information you need.

When a limitation affects interpretation, discuss it in the Discussion but keep it out of the power positions of the opening and resolution, placing it briefly and honestly early in the body before getting on with the story.

On the rare occasions when methods are unusual or novel, open the Discussion with a methodological-considerations section so readers get calibration on the methods' strengths and weaknesses before the results.
condition: when the experimental approach is unusual or novel

statement: Never make a limitation the conclusion, but when you must mention limitations within the conclusions, use a tight but-yes structure that frames the limitation quickly and pushes on to what you learned.

Separate the negatives and positives into different story arcs, placing limitations in a preceding paragraph and the conclusions in the final one, and link them with a phrase such as despite these limitations that both reminds readers of the limits and minimizes them.
Recognize that addressing your work's limitations honestly makes the presentation clear, strong, and credible, motivating others to build on and cite it.

Recognize that story structure transcends language: the hardest part of writing science is developing and laying out the story, which is a matter of structure or knowing what to put where and comes before language, so OCAR is not about English.

Balance confidence and humility in doing and writing science, with confidence to develop and expose your own ideas to criticism and humility to admit the work's limitations, because too much confidence blinds you to the limitations and too much humility blinds you to the accomplishments.
Develop the courage to ask new questions and reach for understanding rather than only presenting results, because leading journals want new knowledge and understanding, not more information.

Recognize that answering an old question in a new system, with new technology, or both does not make science novel and only fills the information base, because novelty lies in the new questions and interpretations that a prior finding leaves open.

Distinguish information from knowledge rather than basic from applied research, because a leading journal rejects work that only fleshes out the information base while first-rate work of either kind provides broader, transferable insight.
Before submitting, know a journal's focus and audience and match the journal to your story by its scope rather than its status, because submitting a paper that does not fit wastes everyone's time.
Recognize that journal prestige means little in the long run, because good papers get found and cited regardless of venue while bad ones are ignored.
Find and highlight the novelty in your own data, because few data sets are so novel they cannot be made dull or so dull they hold no novel insight, and finding the novelty is the hard part.

Take responsibility as the author for submitting correct English with the right words spelled correctly and grammar and usage followed, because reviewers, editors, and publishers will not fix imperfect English and most journals bounce sub-standard language before review.

Use a spell checker but know it misses errors like their versus there and real-but-wrong words like from versus form, treat a grammar checker as only a little better than nothing, and keep good short grammar references at hand.

Do not rely solely on an English-speaking friend to check your language unless they are a skilled editor, because a careful word-by-word edit is hard and time-consuming, and a skilled professional editing service is a small, worthwhile investment.

Ensure an English-speaking coauthor takes responsibility for the paper's language, because all authors are responsible for the entire content and a poorly written paper with a native-speaker coauthor invites brutal reviews.
condition: when a coauthor is a native English speaker

statement: Prioritize the story over the grammar, because an editor will send a strong-story weak-language paper back to be fixed but reject a weak-story paper outright, and you can hire an editor for language but not a scientist for your science.

Treat science as a dialect of English rather than a separate language, so writing for the public requires the same techniques done more (more story and SUCCES) and less (less complexity and jargon), not different ones.

Keep a public story simple and focus it on the who-knew element or the application (what it means for the audience or society), and talk about the people doing the work, because for nonscientists people are more engaging characters than chemicals or concepts.
Use a front-loaded LDR structure for a public audience, because they are impatient and need the SUCCES elements engaged quickly.
condition: when writing for a general public audience

statement: Keep public language simple by defining or avoiding every technical term, never introducing a technical term in the topic position, and never being patronizing, assuming an audience that is intelligent but ignorant and highlighting the simple core in their language.
condition: when writing for a general public audience

statement: Present science to the public as a process of incremental struggle rather than as Eureka breakthroughs, because the best public stories integrate the scientist's joy in puzzling out nature with the audience's focus on results and application.

Frame a story with the message box by setting the Issue and Audience, then moving through Problem (the opening and challenge), So what (why the audience should care), Solution (the action or body), and Benefits (the resolution).

Answer a lay question in the audience's own schema, starting from their concern such as curing cancer, because if you cannot meet them there they leave baffled; frame the answer honestly without grandiose claims.
Use the message box for a peer audience too, because readers of any kind ask the same three questions: what is the problem, what is your solution, and why should I care.

Recognize that communicating clearly is not enough to influence policy makers and managers, because their decisions are shaped by political as much as by natural reality, so effecting change means working in their world rather than expecting them to work in yours.

Speak to decision makers in their language and above all their story structure, because with only a few minutes and an impatient audience they listen most for the wrap-up (what you are asking them to do), so put the ask in the closing position.
condition: when communicating with policy makers or managers

statement: Recognize that policy makers and managers face pressures beyond the science and do not see science in the same terms you do, so being effective in the policy arena requires political skills that go beyond writing tools.
Understand that writing skills cannot replace scientific skills or rescue fundamentally weak research, but they help you identify, facet, and polish the valuable core of a rough, flawed data set.

Ground every specific writing guideline in the two roots of stickiness (SUCCES) and story structure (OCAR), remembering to target your audience, focus on the critical story elements, and treat science as being about knowledge and understanding rather than just data.
Focus on success strategies rather than survival strategies, because clearing the bar of success clears the bar of survival without your noticing it was there.
Treat publish or perish as the basis for survival but not success, because you succeed by being cited rather than by publishing a lot, and the quality of papers ultimately trumps quantity.

Aim to impress your real peers, the people who actually read and cite your work, because their citations, invitations, and promotion letters rather than raw publication counts determine your standing, and quality begets quantity.

Prefer an OCAR structure over topic-sentence-development when developing a complex argument that must carry its own limitations, because TS-D is a weak structure for a complex argument, though TS-D may win when space is at a premium.
Design a research paper around the needs of referees and readers: make it easy to read, make the addressed gap explicit, and distinguish the findings from prior work.
condition: When writing or revising a research paper for publication

statement: Meet disciplinary and journal expectations by organizing content clearly and structuring sections, paragraphs, and sentences deliberately.
condition: When preparing a manuscript for a particular research community

statement: Study many papers from the target field to identify conventional phrases for recurring rhetorical functions and effective patterns of paper structure.
condition: When learning to write for a specific field or genre

statement: Use successful papers from the target field as structural and phrase-level models for a new manuscript.
condition: When the models perform the same rhetorical functions and follow the relevant journal or disciplinary conventions

statement: Remove redundant words and phrases because unnecessary length creates more opportunities for language errors and makes a paper harder to read.
condition: When wording can be shortened without losing scientific content or necessary qualification

statement: Plan the manuscript so readers can follow the logical progression toward each conclusion at both paragraph and sentence level.
condition: When arranging arguments, results, and conclusions

statement: Make every reference to work or findings unambiguous about whether it denotes the authors' contribution or someone else's.
condition: When discussing the literature alongside the current study

statement: Check pronouns and other referring expressions so each one has a single, unmistakable referent.
condition: When revising sentences that use forms such as it, this, these, them, or one

statement: Treat clarity, logical organization, concision, lack of ambiguity, and readability as cross-disciplinary quality criteria even though fields differ in preferred structure and style.
condition: When evaluating research writing across disciplines
exception: Field-specific conventions can still require different structures and presentation choices.

statement: Do not equate grammatical correctness with readability; a grammatically correct manuscript can still be rejected if referees cannot readily understand it.
condition: When assessing the language quality of a manuscript

statement: Use a planned writing method because beginning without one can force extensive restructuring and rewriting later.
condition: When preparing a research manuscript

statement: Before drafting, state the intended contribution concisely and verify that it is genuinely original relative to the field's existing knowledge.
condition: When publication is justified by filling or advancing a knowledge gap

statement: Budget substantially more time for planning and manuscript preparation than the first estimate, rather than compressing writing into a short period after a long research project.
condition: When scheduling preparation of a submission

statement: Evaluate several candidate journals by comparing their style, audience, article types, and editorial expectations before choosing a target.
condition: When the target journal has not already been prescribed

statement: A manuscript may have a better editorial fit when it contributes to a discussion or planned theme already active in the target journal.
condition: When a current discussion or special issue aligns substantively with the research

statement: In some cases, select the journal first and frame the paper around the research angle that genuinely matches that journal's audience and expectations.
condition: When multiple legitimate angles of the completed research are available
exception: Do not distort the research merely to manufacture journal fit.

statement: Obtain the target journal's current author instructions before drafting and follow its requirements rigorously.
condition: When preparing a paper for a named journal

statement: Check journal-specific requirements for title form, section organization, abstract layout, voice, citation and bibliography style, keywords, and spelling convention.
condition: When converting author instructions into a drafting checklist

statement: If the target journal provides weak author resources, consult guidance and well-written papers from a strong journal in the same field for transferable clarity and structure techniques.
condition: When supplementary models do not conflict with the target journal's explicit rules
exception: Target-journal requirements take precedence over external models.

statement: Analyze highly relevant, highly cited, or classic papers with a structured comparison matrix covering problem, background, novelty, method, results, interpretation, strengths, weaknesses, and implications.
condition: When conducting the literature review and positioning a new study

statement: A structured comparison of prior studies can reveal differences in approach and results, limitations or bias in earlier work, and the specific way the current study extends the literature.
condition: When the comparison includes literature directly relevant to the current research question

statement: Read a substantial sample of the target journal to infer what its editors consistently value rather than relying only on generic publication advice.
condition: When assessing editorial fit

statement: Assess whether a manuscript offers a clear purpose, sound and reproducible methods, ethical and unbiased research, acknowledged limitations, and results aligned with its objectives.
condition: When reviewing a manuscript against typical editorial criteria
exception: Exact criteria and acceptable article types vary by journal.

statement: Choose a strong model paper close to the topic and inspect how it opens, allocates content by section, connects paragraphs, links Results to Discussion, and presents conclusions.
condition: When learning the structural conventions of the target research genre

statement: Collect reusable phrases from effective model papers according to the rhetorical job they perform, because familiar disciplinary phrasing can make prose easier for readers to process.
condition: When the phrases are generic and appropriate to the new paper's meaning
exception: Do not copy source-specific wording or content.

statement: Choose the drafting order that best supports the author's reasoning; sections need not be written in their final published sequence and may be developed concurrently.
condition: When planning the writing workflow

statement: Drafting a provisional Abstract early may help orient the manuscript around its central aims and findings, but revise it after the paper is complete.
condition: When the author benefits from an early synthesis of the study

statement: Writing Results and Discussion before the Introduction can clarify the study's actual significance and therefore what background the Introduction must establish.
condition: When the significance of completed work is not yet fully articulated

statement: Maintain separate section files or workspaces with provisional concept lists so ideas discovered while drafting one section can be captured immediately in the relevant section.
condition: When drafting several sections in parallel

statement: Explain the research orally to a non-expert to expose unclear thinking, identify what is genuinely important, and test accessibility for readers outside the narrow specialty.
condition: When the author is struggling to begin or to prioritize the study's message

statement: Present methods and results to colleagues before drafting so they can identify omitted issues, alternative interpretations, anomalous or negative findings, and weakly supported conclusions.
condition: When knowledgeable colleagues are available for constructive critique

statement: Before writing, identify the research goal, the most important findings, the evidence supporting them, and how they differ from and add to prior knowledge.
condition: When deciding whether a study warrants a paper and what message it should carry

statement: Rank the key findings and select those that fit the journal's space limit instead of treating every result as equally central.
condition: When the available word count cannot support every finding at equal depth

statement: For each key finding, investigate plausible alternative explanations and possible author bias, then justify the preferred explanation without presenting it as immune to revision.
condition: When interpreting findings and judging the study's contribution

statement: Plan each major section to answer the relevant parts of five contribution questions: the problem, the approach, its difference from prior approaches, the discoveries, and their relation to and meaning for the literature.
condition: When deciding where and how to present a paper's contribution
exception: The emphasis and detail should vary by section.

statement: Make the central contribution recoverable from several sections because readers may enter a paper through the Abstract, Discussion, figures, tables, or another section rather than reading linearly.
condition: When drafting a paper likely to be scanned selectively
exception: Avoid mechanically repeating identical wording in every section.

statement: During drafting, repeatedly connect content to the contribution to maintain focus; remove excessive highlighting during revision if it becomes repetitive.
condition: When the manuscript's central message is at risk of becoming diffuse

statement: Optimize a manuscript for both specialist scrutiny and comprehension by less-experienced or adjacent-field readers.
condition: When the actual expertise of editors, referees, and readers is uncertain

statement: Use simple language without reducing scientific substance: experts need adequate detail, but complexity of expression is not a substitute for depth.
condition: When explaining specialized research
exception: Necessary technical terms and methodological detail should be retained.

statement: Clear construction and easy reading can matter more to acceptance than flawless sentence-level English when residual errors do not obstruct meaning.
condition: When language errors are minor and comprehension remains intact
exception: Some reviewers may scrutinize grammar and vocabulary closely, so accuracy still matters.

statement: Obtain the target journal's referee report form when possible and turn its evaluation questions into both a drafting guide and a final self-review checklist.
condition: When the review criteria or form can be accessed legitimately

statement: A publication-readiness checklist should test novelty and relevance, journal fit, grammatical clarity, succinct and appropriate style, title-content alignment, abstract accuracy, and evidential support for conclusions.
condition: When performing a pre-submission review
exception: Add any further criteria specified by the target journal.

statement: Draft directly in English with the aid of appropriate model papers rather than first composing in another language and translating sentence by sentence.
condition: When the author can formulate the research adequately in English
exception: Authors who cannot yet draft accurately in English may need additional language or editing support.

statement: Keep research notes in the intended publication language throughout the project because this supplies draft material, builds writing practice, and may expose gaps in understanding before manuscript preparation.
condition: When the intended paper will be written in English

statement: Use targeted feedback on actual research notes or a peer writing group to improve domain-specific English through repeated writing and evaluation.
condition: When suitable reviewers or colleagues are available

statement: In English declarative prose, keep the core sequence of subject, verb, direct object, and indirect object recognizable and keep these elements close together.
condition: When writing ordinary research sentences rather than intentionally marked constructions
exception: Established grammatical constructions can require a different surface order.

statement: Compare sentence patterns in the author's first language with English to identify habitual word-order transfers that impose extra processing on English readers.
condition: When recurring English word-order problems may reflect first-language syntax

statement: Choose the grammatical subject according to the information that deserves focus, often the newest or most relevant information in that context.
condition: When several entities could grammatically serve as the subject
exception: Previously known information may be the correct subject when it is the intended topic.

statement: Use the sentence opening for meaningful topical information and move or compress low-value framing phrases that delay it.
condition: When an introductory phrase adds little information or emphasis
exception: Retain framing that readers need before interpreting the main clause.

statement: When alternative subjects provide the same focus, prefer the one that yields the most concise and direct sentence; an active construction often achieves this.
condition: When active and passive versions preserve the intended emphasis and meaning
exception: Use passive voice when the receiver, procedure, or result appropriately deserves focus.

statement: Replace impersonal openings built around an empty 'it' with a concrete subject, modal verb, or direct passive construction when doing so reveals the proposition sooner.
condition: When impersonal 'it' delays the real subject or action
exception: Retain impersonal constructions when they are idiomatic and improve rather than obscure focus.

statement: Do not introduce a pronoun before naming its referent; sentence-initial pronouns are safe only when an earlier noun makes the backward reference unmistakable.
condition: When using pronouns such as it or they

statement: Normally state what an entity is before describing its importance, evidence, or attributes, rather than postponing the subject until the end of an introductory clause.
condition: When delayed-subject syntax makes readers wait to discover the topic
exception: Use a marked order only when it is grammatical and serves a deliberate discourse purpose.

statement: Keep the subject and its verb close enough that readers can identify the sentence's direction before processing long qualifications or lists.
condition: When a long subject or intervening material separates the core clause

statement: Move substantial parenthetical material away from the subject-verb boundary because it interrupts the logical path and is perceived as secondary.
condition: When more than a brief modifier appears between subject and verb
exception: A short, essential modifier may remain if it cannot be misattached.

statement: Present procedural information in chronological order when that order helps readers reconstruct the sequence, while placing causes or qualifications where the intended emphasis requires.
condition: When sentence parts can be ordered in more than one grammatical way

statement: Keep a verb adjacent to its direct object and normally place the direct object before an indirect object introduced by forms such as to or with.
condition: When using a verb that takes both direct and indirect objects
exception: A conventional double-object construction may use the recipient before the thing transferred.

statement: When a direct object is a long list, reveal its relationship early by attaching the indirect object after the first item, introducing the list with a category label, or formatting the items as a list.
condition: When the normal object order would make readers wait too long for the relationship

statement: Place common one-word frequency adverbs near the verb according to the auxiliary structure, and place them after forms of 'be'.
condition: When positioning ordinary frequency adverbs in an English clause
exception: Some adverbs can move to sentence-initial position for deliberate emphasis.

statement: Place adverbs of certainty immediately before negation so the scope of the probability judgment is clear.
condition: When a certainty adverb modifies a negative proposition

statement: As a reliable default, put manner adverbs after the verb or its direct object rather than in a position where their attachment may be unclear.
condition: When no special emphasis requires a different grammatical position

statement: Replace generic time-first openings with the substantive subject when the time phrase is conventional, predictable, and delays the topic.
condition: When opening an Abstract or Introduction with a broad trend statement
exception: Keep the time frame first when temporal contrast is the intended focus.

statement: When possible, integrate consequence or addition markers inside the clause so the substantive subject remains prominent, and avoid starting a run of sentences with repetitive link phrases.
condition: When repositioning the linker preserves its logical scope
exception: Use an initial linker when readers need the relationship signaled before the proposition.

statement: Place a contrast marker at the start of a sentence when readers need immediate notice that the paragraph's logical direction is changing.
condition: When a new sentence contrasts with the preceding proposition
exception: Some contrast constructions grammatically belong inside a two-part sentence.

statement: Use sentence-initial linkers selectively for enumeration, concession, alternatives, attention, or specification when their signaling value is needed before the proposition.
condition: When the relationship would otherwise be unclear or insufficiently prominent
exception: Delete a specification marker when the sentence remains equally clear without it.

statement: Put an attributive adjective before the noun it modifies; if the description follows the noun, use a predicate or an appropriate relative clause.
condition: When writing an ordinary English noun phrase
exception: Certain established postpositive adjectives follow different conventions.

statement: When a measurement expression modifies a noun, use the conventional singular modifier form and hyphenate the compound where required.
condition: When forms such as an age, distance, or duration function adjectivally before a noun

statement: Place an adjective next to the noun it actually describes; rewrite stacked noun phrases with prepositions when an intervening adjective would attach to the wrong noun.
condition: When a multi-noun phrase makes modifier attachment uncertain

statement: Do not invent long strings of nouns merely for concision; verify that the proposed compound is established in the field and otherwise unpack it with prepositions.
condition: When several nouns are used consecutively to modify a final noun
exception: Retain conventional compounds already standard in the target discipline.

statement: Test each modifier for competing attachments and rewrite so only the intended entity can be interpreted as performing, possessing, or being described by it.
condition: When a participle, prepositional phrase, or purpose clause could modify more than one element

statement: Arrange adjacent words into unmistakable conceptual groups so readers do not initially construct a plausible but wrong interpretation and then have to reprocess the sentence.
condition: When a compact noun phrase or clause boundary creates a temporary ambiguity

statement: State explicitly whether the current findings agree or disagree with a cited author's position instead of relying on a loosely placed attribution phrase.
condition: When comparison wording could attach either to a positive or a negative proposition

statement: Treat repeated moments of reader reinterpretation as a serious readability defect even when each individual ambiguity can eventually be resolved.
condition: When evaluating a manuscript's cumulative processing burden

statement: Prefer short, clear sentences at the beginning of a paper because early difficulty is especially likely to lose readers.
condition: When drafting the opening of a manuscript
exception: A longer sentence is acceptable if its structure remains immediately clear.

statement: Do not bury essential information in the middle of a long sentence, where readers are less likely to give it the attention accorded to sentence boundaries.
condition: When prioritizing information within a sentence

statement: Use roughly 15–18 words as a clarity-oriented sentence-length target and treat about 25 words as a review trigger rather than an absolute maximum.
condition: When editing ordinary academic prose for first-pass comprehension
exception: A longer sentence may remain when its information structure is simple and unambiguous.

statement: Split a sentence that carries several distinct ideas into separate thought units; this can improve clarity while also eliminating words needed only to connect the overloaded structure.
condition: When a reader cannot identify the ideas and their relationships on first reading

statement: Do not assume that complex research ideas require syntactically complex sentences; conceptual depth and simple expression are compatible.
condition: When an author defends long sentences as necessary for scholarly nuance
exception: Some relationships still require carefully controlled subordination or qualification.

statement: Review sentences containing multiple linkers, heavily qualified lists, several semicolons or colons, or many commas for overloaded clause structure.
condition: When screening a draft for sentences likely to be too long or complex
exception: Punctuation count alone does not prove a sentence is unclear.

statement: If an already substantial first clause is followed by another substantial unit, consider ending the sentence before the added unit.
condition: As a heuristic when the first unit is roughly 12–15 words and the added unit roughly 10–12 words or more
exception: Keep the units together when their grammatical dependency is essential and the result remains easy to process.

statement: Use an oral read-through as a diagnostic: a sentence that cannot be spoken comfortably as one unit warrants review for division or restructuring.
condition: When a quick test for excessive sentence load is useful
exception: Breath length is a heuristic, not a grammatical rule.

statement: Distinguish 'and' that joins parallel words from 'and' that adds a new proposition or procedural step; the latter often marks an appropriate sentence boundary.
condition: When revising a sentence with multiple uses of 'and'
exception: Closely coupled propositions may remain in one sentence if their relationship is immediately clear.

statement: In a Methods description, normally limit a sentence to one or two actions or items so readers can distinguish successive procedural steps.
condition: When several procedures are being reported in sequence
exception: Keep tightly integrated actions together when separating them would obscure their functional relationship.

statement: When splitting a sentence joined by an additive phrase that cannot grammatically open the new sentence, restate enough of the previous proposition to make the added explanation independent.
condition: When an additive construction would otherwise create an overlong sentence

statement: When dividing a contrast into two independent sentences, replace a dependent-clause linker with an independent-sentence contrast marker that preserves the relationship.
condition: When the original contrast marker requires two clauses in one grammatical sentence

statement: Use subordinators such as 'although', 'since', and explanatory 'as' only when they introduce a clause grammatically dependent on a main clause.
condition: When expressing concession or cause within one sentence
exception: Use a suitable independent connective when starting a separate sentence.

statement: Avoid making readers hold a long sentence-initial subordinate clause before discovering its main assertion; state the proposition first or split the material and name the relationship explicitly.
condition: When the introductory dependent clause contains substantial information
exception: A short framing clause may remain first when it provides necessary context.

statement: When a sentence combines a problem, a resulting decision, and the concrete actions taken, present those stages as separate sentences in causal order.
condition: When consequence and purpose phrases produce an overloaded sentence
exception: A compact construction may remain when all stages are short and immediately clear.

statement: Use relative clauses for genuinely compact additions, but split a sentence when successive relative clauses introduce multiple new pieces of information.
condition: When a relative clause materially lengthens or redirects the sentence
exception: A short relative clause with an unambiguous antecedent can remain embedded.

statement: Replace an overlong explanatory relative clause with a new sentence beginning with a precise demonstrative noun phrase that names the preceding fact, decision, method, or entity.
condition: When the referent of the new demonstrative is unmistakable
exception: Do not use a bare demonstrative if several possible antecedents exist.

statement: Do not let an embedded relative clause separate a subject from its main verb by so much material that readers may lose the core sentence.
condition: When the embedded material contains several propositions or roughly a clause-length span

statement: When breaking an embedded construction into sentences, order the resulting statements according to the topic that deserves greatest emphasis.
condition: When more than one grammatical restructuring is possible

statement: Prefer an explicit relative clause or a separate sentence over an uncertain reduced-relative construction whose omitted words may make the attachment ungrammatical or ambiguous.
condition: When unsure whether a relative pronoun and form of 'be' can safely be omitted

statement: Repeat a key noun when needed to establish a clean new sentence; controlled lexical repetition is preferable to a compressed but unclear relationship.
condition: When splitting a sentence would otherwise require a vague pronoun or risky ellipsis
exception: Avoid repetition that adds no referential or structural clarity.

statement: When an added participial phrase substantially lengthens a sentence, start a new sentence, repeat or name the subject, and use a finite verb in the appropriate tense.
condition: When an '-ing' phrase adds a distinct result, effect, or attribute
exception: Keep a short participial phrase when its actor and relationship are unambiguous.

statement: Convert a sentence-final participial interpretation into a separate sentence beginning with a precise 'this' expression when the inference deserves independent emphasis.
condition: When a participial phrase reports what the preceding result indicates
exception: Ensure the demonstrative names the exact result or observation being interpreted.

statement: Keep a purpose expression within the action sentence only when the rationale is brief; present a substantial rationale and the action in separate sentences.
condition: When a purpose phrase grows beyond a short, easily processed unit

statement: As a default, state what was done before giving an extended rationale because the action supplies context for interpreting the reason.
condition: When action and rationale must be divided into separate sentences
exception: Lead with the rationale when it is the established topic or needed to understand the action.

statement: Treat numerous clause-separating commas as a signal to reorganize the content, although commas used within a straightforward list are not themselves a problem.
condition: When screening a sentence for excessive informational load
exception: A grammatically controlled list may legitimately contain several commas.

statement: Reorganize an overloaded sentence by placing subordinate ideas in logical order, turning them into separate sentences, and grouping rationale and procedure into distinct paragraphs when appropriate.
condition: When a sentence mixes aims, hypotheses, materials, procedures, examples, and consequences

statement: Accept a higher total word count when restructuring is necessary to make relationships and stages immediately comprehensible.
condition: When a shorter compressed version forces readers to reconstruct the logic
exception: Do not add explanatory wording that is itself redundant.

statement: Break chains of comma-delimited descriptions into sentences that explicitly name what each description modifies.
condition: When each successive phrase could be mistaken for another item in a list or could attach to several antecedents

statement: Prefer a full stop to a semicolon when the second part adds an independent idea and the dependency does not need to be encoded in one sentence.
condition: When either punctuation choice preserves the intended meaning
exception: Use a semicolon when it performs a clear grouping function or prevents list ambiguity.

statement: Use a colon to introduce compact elaboration or a short list, but split the construction if the material before or after the colon already makes the sentence long.
condition: When deciding whether a colon-supported sentence remains readable

statement: Use semicolons inside a short complex list to make subgroup boundaries visible when commas alone would merge the groups.
condition: When list items contain internal conjunctions or commas
exception: For a long or heavily explained list, use separate sentences or displayed formatting instead.

statement: Present a long sequence of components with separate enumerated sentences so readers can recognize the number and boundaries of the components.
condition: When each listed component needs its own explanation
exception: A compact displayed list may be more efficient when the items require little prose.

statement: Reserve parentheses mainly for brief, nonessential examples or short lists that do not interrupt the sentence's logical flow.
condition: When deciding whether information belongs parenthetically
exception: Field-specific notation and citation conventions may require parentheses for other compact functions.

statement: Move an explanatory parenthesis into the main prose or a separate sentence when it materially lengthens the sentence or interrupts the argument.
condition: When the parenthetical content is a proposition rather than a compact example

statement: Dividing a long sentence does not inherently reduce conceptual complexity; it changes the delivery into units that readers can absorb on first reading.
condition: When the same propositions and relationships are preserved across the shorter sentences

statement: Write research prose under a writer-responsibility model: explicitly supply connections so readers need minimal effort to reconstruct the argument.
condition: When communicating in English-language technical and academic genres
exception: Do not over-explain relationships that are already unmistakable to the intended audience.

statement: Design for scanning as well as linear reading by reaching substantive information quickly and ensuring that headings, openings, and other high-attention positions carry value.
condition: When readers are likely to encounter the paper on screen or search it for specific information

statement: Remove words that add no informational or rhetorical value because low-value stretches encourage readers to skip farther or abandon the text.
condition: When revising for selective, time-constrained reading
exception: Retain necessary transitions, qualifications, and definitions even when they do not add a new finding.

statement: Reveal logical relationships incrementally so each word and sentence connects to the next and readers do not have to wait until the end of a sentence, paragraph, or section to assemble the meaning.
condition: When structuring an argument for first-pass comprehension
exception: A deliberate delayed reveal is rarely appropriate in research reporting and must not obscure the claim.

statement: Structure an ordinary body paragraph with a topic sentence linked to the previous context, a short logical development, and a closing sentence that consolidates the point or leads forward.
condition: For a body paragraph that is not serving a special section-opening function
exception: Very short transitional paragraphs or field-specific formats may not need all three elements.

statement: Limit each sentence to one specific idea and each paragraph to one general idea so readers can recognize the hierarchy of the argument.
condition: When organizing expository research prose
exception: A sentence may contain necessary qualifications or closely linked subclaims without becoming multi-topic.

statement: Use repeated key terms to create explicit links between adjacent sentences, especially while narrowing from a general topic to a more specific one.
condition: When the same concept continues across sentence boundaries
exception: Use a new term when the concept genuinely changes or a distinction must be introduced.

statement: Do not replace a repeated technical referent with a synonym merely for variety, because readers may infer an unintended difference in meaning.
condition: When terminological identity is important
exception: Vary wording when the alternatives are unquestionably co-referential and repetition becomes distracting.

statement: Use link words only when they clarify how a sentence qualifies, contrasts with, exemplifies, or otherwise relates to what precedes it.
condition: When the logical relation is not already unmistakable from content and order
exception: Omit linkers that merely decorate the prose or restate an obvious relation.

statement: Use an unusually short sentence selectively to focus attention on a pivotal qualification or conclusion.
condition: When the short sentence carries a high-value point and its relationship is clearly signaled
exception: Frequent isolated short sentences can make prose sound like a list.

statement: Keep no more than one or two main ideas in a sentence so readers can assign appropriate weight to each without unpacking a bundle of claims.
condition: When revising ordinary expository prose
exception: Necessary qualifications may accompany a main idea if they remain subordinate and clear.

statement: Consider opening a major section with a one- or two-sentence recap of the paper's relevant aims or findings so selective readers can orient themselves.
condition: When the section may be read independently and the target journal commonly uses such recaps
exception: Use a direct opening when space is tight or the journal's papers do not use section summaries.

statement: At a section opening, briefly preview the section's sequence when that roadmap materially helps readers understand how its parts fit together.
condition: When the section is long or structurally complex
exception: Omit a roadmap for a short section whose structure is self-evident.

statement: Keep references to later sections concise and use them only to locate the current section within the paper's logical progression.
condition: When a forward reference prevents structural confusion
exception: Avoid repeated navigational prose that burdens the reader.

statement: In a short paper or a section where readers need the result immediately, open with the main finding or meaning rather than a procedural account of how it was obtained.
condition: When methodological detail is already available elsewhere and is not needed to interpret the opening claim
exception: Lead with method when the method itself is the contribution or establishes necessary credibility.

statement: Choose the ratio of background to new information according to the section, the audience's expected knowledge, and the rhetorical goal.
condition: When deciding how directly to introduce a study

statement: Use familiar information at the beginning of a paragraph to establish context, then introduce the problem or novelty that the paper addresses.
condition: When readers need orientation before they can evaluate the new contribution
exception: Skip familiar background when the intended audience can be assumed to know it and attention is the priority.

statement: In a specialized Abstract, move quickly from the current state to its limitation, then report the study, findings, and proposed advance.
condition: When the audience already understands the basic topic and its established methods
exception: Add more context for a broad or cross-disciplinary readership.

statement: An Abstract can begin directly with clear findings or a new method to maximize attention when the venue is highly specialized and the contribution is strong enough to support that opening.
condition: When readers need little background and the study has a definite result or methodological advance
exception: Do not use a findings-first opening when the result is unintelligible without context.

statement: In an English sentence, normally place established or lower-priority information before the new or highest-priority information.
condition: When both pieces form a coherent topic-to-comment progression
exception: Reverse the order when contrast, correction, or a specific emphasis requires it.

statement: Place important information at a sentence boundary rather than in the middle of a long construction, and use the final position to signal the intended informational weight.
condition: When rearrangement preserves the logical relationships

statement: Put a concession marker early when readers must know that the initial information will be qualified by the sentence's main point.
condition: When the main emphasis belongs to the qualification rather than the conceded fact

statement: Give two propositions separate sentences when both deserve equal emphasis rather than subordinating one within the other.
condition: When readers should notice and absorb each proposition independently
exception: Avoid creating a long sequence of equally short, list-like sentences.

statement: Build a paragraph as a general-to-specific chain in which each sentence develops a concept introduced by the previous sentence.
condition: When developing an explanatory or argumentative paragraph
exception: A deliberate return to a higher-level topic should be explicitly signaled.

statement: Make every sentence intelligible from information already supplied, rather than requiring the reader to reach the paragraph's end before understanding an earlier statement.
condition: When sequencing English research prose
exception: A tightly controlled question-and-answer sequence may temporarily defer an answer without making the question unintelligible.

statement: Signal a departure from the argument's main line at the point where the side path begins, not after readers have already followed it.
condition: When introducing a qualification, digression, or secondary analysis

statement: If a paragraph previews categories or stages, explain them later in the same order and at the same level of categorization.
condition: When a paragraph begins with an explicit list or taxonomy
exception: Announce any necessary change of order before making it.

statement: Develop classifications hierarchically: define the whole, name the main categories, complete one category's explanation, then move to the next and its subdivisions.
condition: When explaining a taxonomy or multi-part concept

statement: Forewarn readers of a coming contrast at the start of the construction so they do not initially assign primary importance to a proposition that will immediately be reversed or qualified.
condition: When a sentence contrasts an established feature with the actual novelty

statement: State the interpretive standpoint or relevant condition before the claim when it determines how the claim should be read.
condition: When a phrase such as a statistical viewpoint or operating condition scopes the proposition
exception: A final-position qualifier may be used for deliberate emphasis if it cannot be mistaken as an afterthought.

statement: Express a negative proposition early and place negation directly with the verb so readers do not construct an affirmative interpretation first.
condition: When the intended message is negative

statement: When announcing a fixed number of stages, give each stage its own consistently numbered sentence and carry the numbering through to completion.
condition: When describing a procedure, method, project, or other ordered sequence
exception: Use bullets or a table instead when the stages need substantial nested detail.

statement: Start a new paragraph when shifting from background or prior work to the current study or a key finding so the contribution is visually and rhetorically prominent.
condition: When a contribution-signaling sentence would otherwise be buried inside a long paragraph
exception: A very short paragraph may already provide sufficient prominence.

statement: Break a long block into shorter paragraphs so its main points and their logical sequence are visually identifiable.
condition: When a paragraph contains several stages, comparisons, or shifts in emphasis
exception: Do not split a single tightly unified idea merely to meet an arbitrary visual target.

statement: Use shorter paragraphs as a drafting discipline because they force the writer to identify one main point and express it directly rather than rambling through loosely connected thoughts.
condition: When a draft lacks a clear paragraph-level focus

statement: Shorter paragraphs make later collaboration and space reduction easier because missing information and removable units can be located without modifying an oversized block.
condition: When coauthors revise or the manuscript must be shortened

statement: Treat roughly 8–12 lines or 4–6 sentences as a prompt to recheck paragraph unity, and treat about 15 lines as an approximate upper boundary rather than a hard rule.
condition: When visually reviewing ordinary research paragraphs
exception: Formatting, column width, and the complexity of one coherent idea can justify a different length.

statement: Begin a new paragraph whenever the focus changes, even if the broader topic remains the same.
condition: When moving between another author's approach and the current approach, between compared entities, or between distinct aspects of one topic
exception: A brief contrast or qualification may remain within the paragraph if it does not establish a new focus.

statement: Use purpose, chronology, examples, additions, contrasts, reasons, consequences, mini-conclusions, visual references, enumeration, and topic shifts as diagnostic markers for possible paragraph boundaries.
condition: When the marked function requires several sentences to develop
exception: Do not start a new paragraph for a function expressed completely in one short sentence.

statement: A one-sentence paragraph can be appropriate for special emphasis or transition, but a series of very short paragraphs usually fragments the prose.
condition: When deciding whether a short unit deserves paragraph status

statement: In a literature review, consider paragraph breaks at new historical or logical phases and changes of author; in Methods, use them to separate components or procedural steps.
condition: When section-specific functions provide natural boundaries
exception: Group closely related authors or steps when separating them would hide the comparison or dependency.

statement: Advance directly from the end of one clear paragraph to the next idea rather than inserting a routine mini-summary between every paragraph.
condition: When the logical progression is already explicit
exception: Use a summary where readers need a synthesis before a major transition.

statement: Test a suspected redundant summary by removing it and asking a knowledgeable colleague whether the argument remains easy to follow.
condition: When unsure whether a recap provides navigation or merely repeats content

statement: A synthesis is particularly useful at the end of an Introduction to separate prior-work motivation from the current study, and at the end of a Discussion when no separate Conclusions section exists.
condition: When the section must consolidate its argument or contribution before the paper moves on or ends
exception: Omit it if the journal's format or an already concise structure makes the synthesis redundant.

statement: Avoid ending one section with a preview that is repeated at the opening of the next section.
condition: When both passages convey the same navigation information
exception: A brief cross-reference may remain when readers commonly enter either section independently.

statement: Define concision as expressing the complete necessary meaning with the fewest words, not as deleting scientific content or useful detail.
condition: When shortening research prose

statement: Treat a word, phrase, sentence, paragraph, or subsection as removable when it adds no value to the reader's understanding or use of the paper.
condition: When conducting a substantive concision pass
exception: Retain required methodological detail, qualification, provenance, and journal-mandated content.

statement: Remove redundancy early because readers who encounter padded opening sentences may assume the rest is similarly low-value and switch from close reading to scanning.
condition: When revising an Abstract, Introduction, or other opening passage

statement: Prefer the most concrete available word and remove generic labels that merely restate an attribute already expressed more specifically.
condition: When a generic noun such as process, activity, task, or characteristic adds no distinct meaning
exception: Retain a generic category term when it establishes a needed level in a classification.

statement: Delete adjectives and adverbs that do not change the proposition, and avoid paired modifiers that express essentially the same quality.
condition: When the modifier supplies emphasis without a measurable or interpretive distinction
exception: Retain modifiers that encode scope, degree, uncertainty, comparison, or a defined technical category.

statement: Prefer a direct verb to a nominalization when the verb expresses the same operation more briefly and makes the sentence flow more clearly.
condition: When converting the noun does not erase a meaningful entity or established technical term
exception: Keep a nominalization when the action itself must function as the topic or object of discussion.

statement: Replace a generic helper verb plus action noun with the corresponding single verb to reduce length and avoid collocation errors.
condition: When the single verb preserves tense, agency, and meaning

statement: When the sequence of ideas already makes their relation clear, remove link words that duplicate other markers or repeatedly delay the sentence subject.
condition: When deleting the linker leaves the intended relation unambiguous
exception: Retain or add a linker when it distinguishes evidence, consequence, addition, or another interpretation that readers could otherwise confuse.

statement: Vary the position of necessary linkers rather than beginning several consecutive sentences with them.
condition: When the linker's scope remains clear in a medial position
exception: Keep it initial when readers need the relation before processing the sentence.

statement: Choose the shorter of equivalent words only when it remains appropriately formal and precise for the research context.
condition: When two words genuinely express the same intended meaning
exception: Use the longer term if the shorter alternative is informal, ambiguous, or less technically accurate.

statement: Replace a wordy expression with a shorter grammatical equivalent, especially for comparisons, causal connectors, and attention signals.
condition: When the shorter form preserves the same logical relation and tone

statement: Replace an adjective plus a generic manner noun with the corresponding adverb when this yields a shorter, natural construction.
condition: When the adverb attaches unambiguously to the intended verb or clause
exception: Do not force an awkward adverb when the prepositional phrase conveys a distinct perspective.

statement: Do not repeat a heading's function in the first sentence; begin directly with the results, conclusions, or other content the heading already announces.
condition: When the heading immediately precedes and unmistakably labels the passage
exception: Add orientation if the heading is broad and the subsection's specific purpose is not obvious.

statement: Replace an impersonal 'it is' opening with a modal verb, an evaluative adverb, a named actor, or a rearranged proposition when this brings the subject and claim forward.
condition: When the impersonal construction delays the actual subject or inflates the statement

statement: Retain an impersonal construction when its distance from the author is doing necessary hedging rather than merely adding words.
condition: When the evidential support does not justify a direct or personal assertion
exception: Do not use impersonal phrasing to hide responsibility for a supported methodological choice.

statement: Remove routine authorial commentary about observing, identifying, deciding, turning attention, or finding something interesting, and state the substantive point directly.
condition: When the commentary does not establish a real methodological action, evidential stance, or author responsibility
exception: Retain an explicit author action when agency or choice is material to the research.

statement: Do not use an inclusive author-reader 'we' merely to narrate what a figure or text allows the reader to see; make the figure or evidence the grammatical subject.
condition: When 'we' does not refer to the study's actual authors performing an action
exception: Use 'we' where the journal permits it and author agency genuinely matters.

statement: Refer to a figure or table with a direct active construction and omit generic visual descriptors that merely restate that it is a graphic.
condition: When introducing what a figure or table shows, highlights, or reports
exception: Name a specific visual encoding when it is needed to interpret the evidence.

statement: Do not duplicate in prose all information that readers can readily obtain from a table or figure; report only the patterns and values needed for the argument.
condition: When the visual already presents the detailed data legibly
exception: Repeat a value when it is central to the claim or required for accessibility without the visual.

statement: Express a purpose with a direct infinitive rather than a wordy purpose phrase when the shorter form preserves the exact aim.
condition: When stating why a method, system, or action is used
exception: Use a fuller construction when it distinguishes an intended aim from an actual capability or outcome.

statement: Delete information already encoded by an acronym, tense, location in the paper, or the audience's secure common ground.
condition: When the omitted meaning remains unambiguous in context
exception: Retain expansion, time, location, or background needed by a broader audience or required on first use.

statement: Evaluate every passage from the reader's perspective and remove text retained mainly because the author enjoys its style rather than because it advances understanding.
condition: During substantive revision
exception: Rhetorical interest may remain when it serves comprehension, emphasis, or the genre's legitimate voice.

statement: Put clarity ahead of concision whenever compression would produce an unfamiliar noun string, ambiguous reference, or otherwise unintelligible phrase.
condition: When the shortest wording is harder to interpret than a slightly longer alternative

statement: Vary sentence form and length enough to avoid monotony; an occasional long or complex construction is acceptable when it remains controlled and clear.
condition: When revising an otherwise highly compressed passage
exception: Do not retain complexity solely for stylistic prestige.

statement: Resolve ambiguity when it can alter a reader's understanding of the contribution, evidence, or action, but do not expand every harmless expression into legalistic precision.
condition: When prioritizing ambiguity fixes
exception: A minor alternative reading may remain if it cannot affect the paper's substantive interpretation.

statement: A deliberately vague formulation can be appropriate when the evidence itself does not support a more exact interpretation.
condition: When the author is genuinely uncertain about the meaning or scope of findings
exception: Do not use vagueness to conceal a known limitation, unsupported claim, or avoidable methodological detail.

statement: Distinguish nonrestrictive relative clauses that add optional information from restrictive clauses that identify which members of a set are meant.
condition: When choosing relative-clause form and punctuation

statement: Set a nonrestrictive relative clause off with commas and use an appropriate relative pronoun; use an unpunctuated restrictive clause to supply essential identifying information.
condition: In formal scientific English where the distinction affects meaning
exception: Specific journal dialect and style may permit additional restrictive relative forms.

statement: Rewrite a relative-clause sentence explicitly when punctuation and pronoun choice alone may not make the all-versus-subset distinction obvious to the audience.
condition: When an instruction or claim changes materially depending on whether the clause is restrictive

statement: Place a relative pronoun immediately after the noun it refers to; otherwise readers will normally attach it to the nearest noun.
condition: When using which, that, or who

statement: If intervening material makes a relative pronoun appear to modify the wrong noun, move the clause next to its antecedent or split the sentence and repeat the key noun.
condition: When the intended antecedent cannot remain adjacent in the original structure

statement: Use a participial modifier directly after its noun only when that adjacency makes the actor or referent unambiguous.
condition: When an '-ing' phrase functions like a relative clause
exception: Use an explicit relative clause when another nearby noun could be interpreted as the actor.

statement: Replace a dangling or uncertain participial phrase with a finite clause that names its subject.
condition: When the nearest noun is not the entity performing the participial action

statement: Avoid opening with a bare participial phrase when readers cannot identify its actor until the main clause; use a subject-plus-verb condition instead.
condition: When the grammatical subject of the main clause does not clearly perform the opening action
exception: A standard introductory participial phrase may remain when its subject is unquestionably the main-clause subject.

statement: Use 'by' before a participial phrase to express means, and a consequence marker to express a result; do not leave the relationship implicit when either reading is plausible.
condition: When an '-ing' phrase could describe either how an outcome occurs or what follows from it

statement: When a participial phrase simply adds another proposition, coordinate it with a finite verb or make it a separate sentence.
condition: When no causal, instrumental, or modifying relation is intended

statement: Use the definite article with a countable noun only when the context identifies a specific previously established referent; use an indefinite or generic form for a new class member or a class in general.
condition: When article choice affects whether a noun is interpreted as known and specific
exception: Proper names, mass nouns, and fixed expressions follow additional article conventions.

statement: Do not open a section with a definite countable noun unless readers can identify the referent without searching earlier sections.
condition: When the noun has not been locally introduced
exception: A globally unique or conventionally known referent may take the definite article on first mention.

statement: Use 'one' when the numerical count or contrast with additional instances matters, and an indefinite article when merely introducing a single instance.
condition: When the choice changes whether a larger planned series is implied

statement: Keep uncountable nouns singular and use singular determiners and pronouns; a false plural can redirect later references to the wrong noun.
condition: When English treats the referenced concept as a mass noun
exception: Use a countable unit or subtype noun when distinct items genuinely need enumeration.

statement: Repeat an uncountable noun rather than using a plural-looking pronoun that could refer to another nearby plural noun.
condition: When reference could otherwise be misassigned
exception: A singular pronoun is sufficient when its antecedent is immediate and unique.

statement: When an English pronoun could refer to more than one preceding noun or forces readers to retrieve a distant antecedent, repeat the intended noun.
condition: When pronoun gender, number, or position does not uniquely resolve the reference
exception: Use the pronoun when the antecedent is immediate and unmistakable.

statement: Replace a pronoun with the exact noun or noun set when several listed antecedents make its scope uncertain.
condition: When forms such as one, this, these, them, or they could denote different items or combinations
exception: Retain the pronoun when its antecedent and scope are immediate and unique.

statement: Name whether a consequence applies to one option or to all options rather than leaving a demonstrative to cover an unspecified part of a preceding list.
condition: When a consequence follows alternatives or multiple actions

statement: Avoid 'the former' and 'the latter' when more than two candidates exist, the pair is distant, or the intended grouping is not obvious; repeat the exact term instead.
condition: When a backward reference would require rereading to resolve
exception: The forms may be acceptable for an immediate, unmistakable two-item contrast.

statement: Prefer a repeated specific term to a generic backward-reference label because the specific term is more memorable and carries more informational impact.
condition: When replacing a generic reference such as the former, the latter, or the last topic

statement: Do not use 'above' or 'below' alone when readers may need to retrieve the referenced material; give a section, paragraph, point, table, or other exact location.
condition: When the cross-reference is intended to help readers find supporting content
exception: A vague backward cue is acceptable when it only acknowledges deliberate repetition and no lookup is needed.

statement: Use 'respectively' to establish one-to-one mapping between two ordered item lists when readers might otherwise infer shared or different pairings.
condition: When item order unambiguously determines the intended pairs
exception: Spell out the pairs when the lists are long or the order itself could be misunderstood.

statement: Use punctuation around 'and' to expose grouping when the scope of a following condition or modifier could attach to the whole coordination or only its final member.
condition: When coordination has legally, methodologically, or logically different readings
exception: Prefer a full rewrite if punctuation alone does not make the grouping unmistakable.

statement: Use semicolons to separate groups within a list when commas and conjunctions would obscure which items belong together.
condition: When each list group contains multiple internally coordinated items
exception: Use displayed lists for long or deeply nested groupings.

statement: Use an inclusive coordination when both alternatives apply and an exclusive coordination when exactly one alternative applies.
condition: When choosing between 'both…and' and 'either…or'
exception: If the intended 'or' is inclusive, state that explicitly rather than relying on conversational convention.

statement: Check the placement of inclusive and exclusive correlatives because moving them can change whether they quantify entities, locations, actions, or alternatives.
condition: When a correlative expression appears near multiple possible constituents

statement: Check apparent cognates from the author's first language when an English word may carry a different technical action or degree, such as regulating versus merely checking.
condition: When a familiar-looking word is being used in a consequential methodological or legal statement

statement: Use a defining abbreviation to supply an exhaustive restatement and an example marker to introduce only some members of a larger set.
condition: When choosing between 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' or their prose equivalents

statement: Prefer plain-English equivalents to Latin expressions unless the expression is standard in the target journal and reliably understood by its readership.
condition: When a Latin phrase is not a required technical term
exception: Follow the journal's convention, including italicization, for accepted Latin terms.

statement: Use one stable term for each key concept throughout a paper rather than rotating among synonyms for stylistic variety.
condition: When terminological consistency helps readers track a scientific entity or construct
exception: Use distinct terms only when they encode a real and defined distinction.

statement: If similar terms are intended to have different meanings, define the distinctions before relying on them.
condition: When multiple near-synonyms are necessary in the same conceptual area

statement: Do not replace a distant technical term with a generic category word such as compound or metal if readers may need to look backward to identify the entity.
condition: When several possible members of the generic category have been mentioned
exception: Use the category term when the generalization itself is intended.

statement: Repeat the shared head noun across coordinated modifiers rather than substituting a vague 'one' when the elliptical form sounds unnatural or could be misread.
condition: When comparing technical subtypes or parameters
exception: A standard compact coordination may omit the repeated head when its grammar and meaning are clear.

statement: Vary generic reporting verbs or evaluative adjectives when repetition becomes heavy, while keeping technical keywords stable.
condition: When the alternatives preserve stance, intensity, and meaning
exception: Do not vary terms if the alternatives imply different evidential strength.

statement: Report an exact quantity when it is available and relevant instead of an indefinite phrase such as a number of cases.
condition: When the quantity affects interpretation, reproducibility, or evidential weight
exception: Use a concise approximate expression when the exact count is unavailable or immaterial.

statement: When using frequency qualifiers such as usually or normally, explain or quantify the exceptional cases if readers need them to interpret the procedure or result.
condition: When exceptions could change reproducibility or the conclusion
exception: No elaboration is needed if the qualifier is incidental and exceptions have no substantive consequence.

statement: Replace relative time labels with dates or defined intervals when the interpretation could change as the paper ages.
condition: When using expressions such as recently, in the near future, or in the short term
exception: A relative label may remain when anchored explicitly to the study period or publication date.

statement: Replace subjective degree words with measurements, comparison baselines, or explicit criteria whenever the degree matters to the claim.
condition: When words such as relatively, substantially, adequate, significant, or suitable are open to materially different readings
exception: Retain a conventional qualitative category when it has been operationally defined.

statement: State the population, location, or domain to which a general-looking claim applies rather than assuming readers share the author's local context.
condition: When a statement could be read as global or as limited to the study setting

statement: Use the most concrete term that fits the intended level of generality, and remove an abstract category phrase when the following definition already names the actual variables or action.
condition: When a generic label is immediately followed by its complete specific meaning
exception: Retain the category if it is needed to organize several later instances.

statement: Make it explicit throughout a paper whether a method, result, or interpretation belongs to the current study, a cited study, or established field knowledge.
condition: When discussing the literature alongside the authors' own work

statement: Check the target journal's policy before choosing first-person or impersonal style, and apply the permitted style without sacrificing ownership clarity.
condition: When drafting or revising authorial references
