A note is only as valuable as the note and reference networks it is embedded in.
Do not worry about completeness: the slip-box is a tool to think with, not an encyclopaedia, so never write a note merely to bridge a gap in a sequence; write only if it helps your own thinking.
Accept that you cannot have an overview of the whole slip-box, just as you cannot have an overview of your own thinking while thinking; it is the medium you think in, not something you think about.

After adding a note, make it findable through the index, but choose keywords carefully and sparingly, because the references between notes matter far more than the references from the index to a single note.

Do not rely exclusively on the index, because that would mean always knowing up front what you are looking for; the slip-box's value is surprising you and reminding you of forgotten ideas through interconnected notes, so most notes are found through other notes and the index need only supply a few entry points.

Structure a topic on a note rather than on a meta-hierarchical level: an overview of a topic is itself just another temporarily valid note bound to change with your understanding, so link the index to it and rewrite it when it no longer represents the cluster.

Choose keywords like a writer, not an archivist: ask in what circumstances you will want to stumble upon this note rather than which category it belongs to, and assign keywords with an eye to the topics you are working on, never by looking at the note in isolation.

Good keywords are usually not words already present in the note, so keyword assignment cannot be automated or delegated to a program; it is a crucial part of thinking that often deepens the note itself and its connections.
Making good cross-references between notes is a matter of serious thinking and a crucial part of developing thoughts, not a mechanical or auto-suggested act.

Maintain overview or entry notes that collect links to the relevant notes on a topic, each with a short indicator, as an in-between step toward a manuscript that helps you orient within the slip-box, building them up organically over time.

What you consider relevant to a topic depends on your current understanding and should be taken seriously, because it defines an idea as much as the facts it rests on; that judgement changes over time and is captured on a new note rather than by discarding the old.

Plain note-to-note links across different locations and contexts act like weak social ties, rarely your first resort but often the source of new perspectives, letting surprising cross-domain patterns emerge that a system separated by preconceived themes could never reveal.

Making links is not file-box maintenance but a crucial part of thinking, and working with actual external notes, where you can see in black and white whether a connection makes sense, makes you less prone to imagine connections that are not there.

The external slip-box structure, shaped by your thinking, in turn shapes your thinking and keeps you grounded, acting as a down-to-earth partner that forces you to check the reference and how a lofty idea connects to the facts you already have.

A system that confronts you with already-thought thoughts reveals that you often have the same idea twice or mistake another person's idea for your own, which is disillusioning but increases the chance you actually move forward instead of just feeling like you do.

Comparing notes side by side reveals small but crucial differences, such as two authors using the same concept slightly differently, that you could not detect from memory alone, and clarifying such differences is a major part of serious academic work.

The brain is good at spotting similarities and differences but needs them presented objectively and externally, because it is much easier to see differences and similarities than to detect them by mere thinking.

Comparing notes helps detect contradictions, paradoxes, and oppositions, which are important facilitators of insight: a contradiction signals a problem worth solving, and the deliberate construction of oppositions is a reliable way to generate new ideas.

Adding a note constantly re-examines old notes in a new light, leading to corrections, complements, and improvements and often disclosing weaknesses in the texts you read, so be extra critical as a reader and always check the original source of a claim.

The slip-box counters the feature-positive effect, our tendency to overweight information that is mentally easily available and most recently acquired, by constantly reminding us of long-forgotten information we would not otherwise recall or even look for.

Flashcards beat cramming but leave each item isolated and un-elaborated, disconnected from any network of theoretical frames or mental models, which makes information both harder to learn and harder to understand in its implications.

A scientific term or concept only becomes meaningful within the context of a theory, and likewise our ability to read a situation depends on our broader knowledge, so meaning is context-dependent rather than intrinsic to an isolated fact.

Assemble a broad toolbox of versatile mental models, taking the most powerful concepts from many disciplines and understanding them so thoroughly they become part of your thinking, because isolated facts banged back are not knowledge in a usable form.
Keep a broad range of mental models rather than just one or two, or you become the man with a hammer who sees nails everywhere, attached to a few models and seeing only what fits them.

A wise person is not someone who knows everything but someone who can make sense of things by drawing on an extended set of interpretation schemes, so it is better to learn from others' reflected experience turned into versatile mental models than only from your own experience.

Practising learning as building a latticework of mental models rather than accumulating isolated facts makes you co-evolve with the slip-box, building the same connections in your head as you develop them externally, and enters a virtuous circle where learning facilitates learning.

Learning is strengthened by elaboration plus retrieving information at different times (spacing), in different contexts (variation), with the help of chance (contextual interference), and with deliberate effort (retrieval).

The slip-box forces you to follow these proven learning practices just by using it, because you elaborate in order to write, retrieve when you connect new notes with old ones, and shuffle contexts and retrieve at irregular intervals along the way.
Creativity is largely connecting things and seeing relationships others miss, rather than a mysterious flash of insight.
All good ideas need time: even sudden breakthroughs are usually preceded by a long, intense process of preparation and prolonged hard thinking about the problem.
Create experimental spaces where ideas can mingle freely and give birth to new ones, and use the slip-box as such a space.

Innovation is usually incremental, many small moves in the right direction rather than one big idea, so the search for small differences between similar concepts and unexpected connections between different ideas is key.

Having concrete notes in front of you to compare directly makes even small differences much easier to spot, because comparing is our natural form of perception and the brain notices details by scanning rather than fixating on one point.

To play with ideas you must first free them from their original context through abstraction and re-specification; abstraction is not the final goal but a necessary in-between step that makes heterogeneous ideas compatible and applicable to new, always-different situations.

The ability to find functional, working solutions equals the ability to abstract: the better you abstract from a specific problem, the better and more pragmatic your solution becomes, even for the very problem you abstracted from.

The real enemy of independent thinking is your own inertia rather than external authority, and generating new ideas is more about breaking old habits of thinking than about producing as many ideas as possible.

The brain makes new information fit the known or drops it from perception to protect its routines, usually without your noticing, so you need a ruse such as an external system to break the power of thinking routines.

Make sure you really see what you think you see and describe it as plainly and factually as possible, double-checking if necessary, because perception interprets instantly, always seeing something as something, rather than seeing first and interpreting second.

Understanding a text is a constant revision of your first interpretation, so train yourself to hold back the urge to jump to conclusions; seeing what is actually there is a learnable skill rather than the trait of open-mindedness, and self-described open-minded people are often more prone to stick to their first reading.

No technique reveals what is missing, but you can make it a habit to always ask what is not in the picture yet could be relevant, guarding against survivorship bias, where the surviving cases can only show what is less relevant.

It is very valuable to know what has already proven not to work, so because our culture over-focuses on success and neglects the lessons of failure, deliberately study failures and the mistakes of others.

Ask counterfactual what-if questions and rediscover the problems for which you already have solutions, because problems are rarely solved directly and the crucial move is usually to redefine the problem so that an existing solution can be employed.
Direct the first question at the question itself: what kind of answer can you expect from asking a question in this particular way, and what is missing from that framing?

Take simple ideas seriously, because grasping an idea is not the same as understanding it and simple is not the same as easy; the worst thing you can do is make a simple task unnecessarily complicated, and needless complexity is often a way to avoid the underlying complexity of simple ideas.
Simple ideas can be tied together into consistent theories and build up enormous complexity, which does not work with complicated ideas.

Restrict yourself to one idea per note in a single plain format, treating even a digital note as if space were limited so it fits on one screen without scrolling, because the one-idea-per-note limit is the precondition for recombining notes freely later.

Self-imposed restriction is liberating: less choice can increase productivity, freedom, and presence, because not having to make choices frees potential that would otherwise be wasted on making those choices.

Thinking and creativity flourish because of structure and restriction, not despite it, as standardised experiments enabled science and strict forms enable poetry; a clear structure lets you explore something's internal possibilities and is even the precondition for breaking with convention, whereas a more complex structure does not provide more possibilities.

The biggest threat to creativity and scientific progress is a lack of structure and restrictions, because without them you cannot differentiate, compare, or experiment and are never forced to decide what is worth pursuing, making indifference the worst environment for insight.

When developing a draft, narrow the perspective to one topic and cut everything that does not directly support the main argument, the opposite of the widening, connection-seeking mode used while building the slip-box.

The brain prioritises ideas that are easily available in the moment, favouring recent, emotional, vivid, and concrete information, which does not equal relevance, making brainstorming a poor way to generate ideas for intellectual work.
Group brainstorming usually produces fewer good ideas and inadvertently restricts the group to a narrower range of topics than individuals working alone.

Topic-finding stops being a problem when you work with the slip-box, because you have already answered what to write about many times a day, and it is far easier to see what worked than to predict what might work.

Let questions arise from the slip-box so they have been tried and tested against dozens of alternatives by trial and error rather than planning, since most possible questions quietly die for lack of interest or material.

A good question sits in the sweet spot of being relevant and interesting, not too easy to answer but tackleable with material within reach, and you cannot judge a question by thinking alone; you must work an idea by writing, connecting, differentiating, and elaborating before you know enough to judge it.

You become more open to new ideas the more intimately familiar you are with existing ones, because only intense elaboration reveals their limitations and lets you modify and genuinely extend them instead of repeating old ideas believing they are new.

Groundbreaking work comes from deep engagement with a problem rather than from an open-minded hobbyist, and the more time devoted to learning about a problem, the more creative the eventual solution is judged to be.

Motivation and the feeling of being in control of one's own learning are among the strongest predictors of student success, and students most often fail when they lose meaning, cannot connect the work to personal goals, or cannot steer their studies autonomously.
Reduce the risk of losing interest in a long project by using a flexible organisation scheme that lets you change course whenever necessary.

Accompany every step of work with the question of what is interesting about it and every reading with what is relevant enough to note down, which both selects information by interest and develops new interests through elaboration.

Opportunistically changing direction is a real form of control, unlike clinging to a plan, so break the big task into small concrete tasks to actually be in control; the more you can steer toward what is interesting, the less willpower you need and the more the work itself becomes the source of motivation.
Autonomous choice among options you personally value energises you and enhances your motivation for later tasks, whereas choice among trivial or irrelevant options can be depleting.

Structure the draft visibly but keep it flexible: the point is less to decide once and for all what goes where than to see what does not need to go in a given part; the structure of an argument is part of the argument and changes as it develops, so treat even a settled table of contents as a guideline, not a prescription.
At the draft stage the problem is the opposite of the blank screen: you have so much material at hand that you must curb the impulse to mention everything at once.

Work on multiple manuscripts at once so the by-products of one project feed others in an intertwined system, letting you progress on future work while on the current one and switch whenever you get stuck or bored, redirecting resistance to another productive goal instead of pushing against it so you never hit a mental blockage.

Be sceptical of planning that focuses on the outcome rather than the actual work and the steps required, because picturing yourself as the successful author does not help but having a realistic idea of what must be done does, just as athletes benefit from imagining the training rather than the win.

You can only learn from experience if feedback follows shortly afterward and more than once, so breaking writing a paper into small tasks provides hundreds of feedback cases a year that make your productivity estimates realistic, unlike merely missing a deadline once in a while.

Work expands to fill the time allotted for long time frames (Parkinson's law), but a task completable in one go tends to speed up as the finish line comes into sight, so the most important step is to get started, which is far easier when the next step is concrete such as writing a note than when it is vague such as keep working on the paper.

Treat the first draft as only the first draft: convince yourself you are merely jotting ideas for yourself that you might make publishable later, which frees you to write, so that by the time you stop the only thing left is to revise.

Rigorously delete whatever has no function in the argument, and make it easier by moving each cut passage into a separate rest document you tell yourself you will reuse later, even though you never do.
Intentions predict behaviour only in the immediate future, while long-run behaviour is predicted by past behaviour rather than intention, so good intentions do not last.

The strongest habits produce the most overconfidence about controlling them, so familiarity makes you feel more in control of exactly the behaviours you control least, which is why behavioural change should start from a realistic idea of how hard it is.

Do not try to break old habits or force change with willpower; strategically build new habits to replace the old ones, starting with the routine of fetching pen and paper to note the important aspects whenever you read, after which the later steps follow because the advantages become obvious quickly.
The slip-box is not just a tool to write more efficiently but also a training device for serious long-term learning.

Talk of innovative learning approaches is idle without changing the actual workflow, and some seemingly innovative ideas such as the learner-centred approach do more harm than good because they still neglect the need for an external scaffolding to think in.
The slip-box does not put the learner at the centre; it lets the learner's own thinking become decentralised within a network of other ideas.

Learning, thinking, and writing should not be about accumulating knowledge but about becoming a different person with a different way of thinking, achieved by questioning one's own thinking routines in the light of new experiences and facts.

Using the slip-box as a mere archive from which you only take out what you put in, without changing the work routines around it, leads to disappointment; reaping its benefits requires changing your routines, grounded in a deep understanding of how and why it works.
Start the note system early rather than only when you are already struggling near a thesis, because it helps far more the earlier you begin, much like saving for retirement.

It is hard to change behaviour under stress, because the more pressure we feel the more we cling to old routines even when those routines caused the problem (the tunnel effect), and the way out is that change becomes possible when the solution appears simple.

The whole method reduces to a simple core: read with a pen in hand, take smart notes, and make connections between them, from which ideas and writing develop by themselves; you never start from scratch, so keep reading, thinking, and writing while taking smart notes along the way.
Even though the research on ego depletion is currently in turmoil, using willpower is a terrible strategy for getting things done in the long run.
Externalise small but important things, because we routinely forget them when we do not, which is why checklists are so valuable wherever something serious is at stake.
Sleep aids memorisation and can help you find solutions to problems.
You are less prone to a cognitive bias such as the feature-positive effect if you are made aware that it exists.
Avoid the productivity loss of group brainstorming by having each member brainstorm individually and compiling the results afterward.
Restraint in preparation, simplicity in design, and naturalness in delivery are the three guiding principles of an effective presentation.
Design of presentation visuals should begin in the preparation stage before opening presentation software, not be added at the end.
Design differs from decoration: the best design goes unnoticed because it makes the message clear rather than drawing attention to itself.
Slides are visual support for a live talk and should not be built to convey the whole message without the presenter present.
Do not merge an oral presentation and a written document into one artifact; combining them produces both a poor presentation and a poor document.
Avoid projecting on a slide the same words the presenter is speaking aloud, because redundant on-screen text harms rather than helps the message.
Audiences find it harder to process information when it is delivered simultaneously in spoken and written form, per cognitive load theory.
Visuals are more memorable than words, whereas bullet points typically add little to a slide.
Replace ubiquitous bulleted-list slide templates with more visual, deliberately designed slides.
Focus on the few important design principles such as restraint and simplicity rather than trying to master software features.
Multimedia slides are not appropriate for every situation; for a small audience with data-intensive material, a handout with discussion or a whiteboard can be more effective.
condition: the audience is small and the material is data-intensive

statement: Use storytelling and narrative to make content engaging and memorable, because people are wired to tell and receive stories.
Before the talk, synthesize the material to find the big picture and decide what matters, letting go of the rest.
Apply empathy by taking the audience's perspective and reading whether they understand, adjusting delivery accordingly.
Appropriate humor and playfulness can make many presentations more engaging and palatable.
condition: in many public-speaking situations

statement: Effective communication increasingly requires right-brain aptitudes (design, story, symphony, empathy, play, meaning) alongside logical analysis.
Design slides to reinforce the presenter's spoken words, not to repeat them.
Slides should demonstrate, with emotional proof, that what the presenter says is true, not merely accurate.
Drastically limit the number of words on a slide; Seth Godin proposes a ceiling of about six words per slide so the slide supports rather than scripts the talk.
Use professional stock photography rather than cheesy or clip-art images.
Avoid gratuitous slide transitions such as dissolves and spins; keep visual mechanics simple.
Provide a detailed written leave-behind document handed out after the talk rather than distributing printouts of the slides.
Pair each slide image with the spoken point so the image triggers an emotional reaction and becomes a memory cue for what was said.
A presentation's purpose is to transfer emotion and sell an idea, not merely to deliver facts; when only facts are needed, send a document instead.
condition: when the aim is to persuade or move an audience rather than merely transmit facts

statement: Effective presenting today requires visual literacy — understanding how imagery conveys messages — not just text literacy.
Study proven visual-storytelling forms such as documentary film and comics to learn presentation technique, rather than relying only on presentation-skills or software books.
A good live presentation has more in common with a documentary film or a comic than with a static bulleted business document.
Treat preparing a presentation as a creative, right-brain act, not merely the linear assembly of facts and data.
Approach presentation preparation with a beginner's mind — open and willing to be wrong — rather than an expert's mind bound by habit.
Treat constraints and limitations as an ally rather than an enemy, because more constraints tend to reveal better design solutions.
Impose your own self-constraints on time, word count, and slide count to force clearer, more focused messages.
Practise tight fixed formats such as Pecha-kucha (20 slides shown for 20 seconds each) to force a brief, focused story.
Do only what is necessary to convey what is essential, and eliminate elements that distract from or obscure the essential whole.
Keep simplicity, clarity, and brevity in mind throughout the preparation of a presentation.
Plan the presentation away from the computer first — sketching ideas on paper ('going analog') — before building slides in software.
Identify the single core message and the big picture before designing any slides.
The best presentation software gets out of the way and amplifies the presenter's own ideas rather than dictating structure through templates.
Slideware templates and wizards impose a cognitive style that oversimplifies content and obscures the message.
Put ideas and structure on a wall using large paper or sticky notes so you can see the whole presentation at once and judge what is essential versus cuttable.
Make deliberate, unhurried time away from the computer to find clarity and the core message, because busyness kills creativity.
Do not optimize for a fixed number of slides or bullets per slide; slide count is not a meaningful quality metric and a successful audience will not notice it.

Before designing slides, answer key planning questions about the audience, context, purpose, and desired action (available time, venue, who the audience is, why you were asked, what you want them to do).
Keep two questions central throughout preparation: What is my point? and Why does it matter to this audience?
Tailor content to the specific audience and occasion; do not reuse slides built for a different audience.
Apply a 'so what?' test to every element and cut any content that does not advance the core message.
Use the elevator test — be able to sell the core message in 30 to 45 seconds — and practise compressing the talk to a fraction of its time.
Prepare a detailed standalone handout during preparation so you can keep the slides simple and need not say everything in the talk.
Treat a presentation as three separate components — slides, speaker notes, and handout — so detailed text and data go into notes or the handout rather than onto the slides.
Never distribute printed copies of your slides as a handout, especially before the talk, because slides are speaker-support material that cannot stand alone.
Do not merge slides and a document into a 'slideument'; a slide-document hybrid produces both poor visuals and poor documentation.
Projected slides should be as visual as possible and support points quickly, while the verbal proof, evidence, and emotion come mostly from the spoken word.
A takeaway handout should provide at least as much depth as the live talk, and often more since people read faster than a speaker talks.
exception: unless the full material is already available in a published book or paper, in which case the handout can be concise and point there

statement: For a short live talk, do not paste full detailed data tables and charts onto slides; show only the parts of the data that truthfully and accurately support the point and put the full data in the handout.
condition: for a short live talk with data-intensive material

statement: On a slide use a simplified chart that supports the point, and reserve detailed charts and tables for the takeaway document where there is room to lay them out properly.
Prepare well enough that you can still deliver your core message without slides, for example if the projector fails or the client asks for it straight.
Give the core message and its supporting messages a logical structure before moving from analog sketches to digital slides.
Design messages to be memorable using the six 'sticky' principles — simplicity, unexpectedness, concreteness, credibility, emotion, and stories (SUCCESs).
Guard against the Curse of Knowledge — as an expert you cannot easily imagine the audience's lack of your background — by avoiding abstractions and making ideas concrete.
Ruthlessly simplify the message to its absolute core: if everything is presented as important, nothing is.
Gain attention by violating the audience's expectations, then sustain curiosity by opening a gap in their knowledge and filling it.
Use concrete images, real examples, and plain language rather than vague abstractions.
Statistics are not inherently persuasive; give numbers context and meaning and frame them so the audience can visualize them.
Make the audience feel something; images create a more visceral, emotional connection than bullet points or data alone.
Wrap ideas in stories and concrete examples, because stories get attention and are easier to remember than lists of facts or rules.
Structure a story with a clear beginning, engaging middle, and clear conclusion.
Internalize your story rather than memorizing it line by line; authentic delivery requires that you genuinely believe it.
Deliver meaning, synthesis, context, and perspective rather than just information, since facts alone are now freely available and no longer a differentiator.
Speak in a natural, conversational human voice rather than formal speech, because audiences stay engaged with conversational narrative.
Avoid slideware's default outline-and-bullet-points structure, which makes content forgettable for the audience.
Storyboard the presentation — on paper, Post-its, or the Slide Sorter view — to visualize the sequence and flow before finalizing slides.
Follow a staged preparation process: brainstorm analog, group ideas to identify the single core theme, storyboard, then build slides.
Aim for about three sections as a manageable, memorable structure, but keep exactly one central theme that every section supports.
condition: three sections is a target, not a fixed rule

statement: Structure the talk as an introduction that presents the issue or 'pain' and the core message, followed by sections that resolve it without ever losing sight of that core.
Use section-divider ('bumper') slides in a contrasting color so sections stand out in the slide sorter and give visual closure between sections.
During brainstorming, generate a large quantity of ideas quickly — words, diagrams, or scenes — going for quantity before quality.
Capture one idea per sticky note with a marker; if an idea needs more space or detail than that, it is too complex.
Do not settle for the first idea that comes to mind; push through four or five more ideas, since stronger solutions frequently appear later.
Expect to discard nearly all the ideas you generate and keep only one; this destructive editing is a healthy part of the creative process.
Avoid cheesy or clichéd metaphor images such as hands shaking in front of a globe; push for original, out-of-the-box visuals.
Walk a colleague through your sketches for feedback in the context of your audience and style before executing them.
Enlist a professional designer when you lack the skills to execute an idea digitally, because effective communication matters more than doing it yourself.
Keep the talk as short as it can be while still doing the job, then go back and edit ruthlessly, cutting anything not crucial to the point — when in doubt, cut it out.
Cut an element even if you are proud of it or it was hard to create, if it does not support your overall point.
Do not include everything 'just in case' out of fear; covering yourself by adding every possible detail is the wrong motivation for content decisions.
Simplicity means clarity, directness, essentialness, and minimalism — not oversimplification or dumbing-down — and achieving it is hard, not easy.
Do not make a visual too simple; make everything as simple as possible but no simpler, because simplicity is not a panacea.
exception: when further simplification would remove essential content or meaning

statement: Make the projected visuals an integral part of the talk that flows with it, not ornamentation sitting off to the side.
Interact with your slides naturally and avoid turning your back on the audience to read them.
Apply kanso: achieve the maximum effect with the minimum means, gaining visual elegance through elimination and omission.
Apply restraint (shizen): include only what is necessary to communicate the message to this audience, avoiding elaborate design and over-refinement.
Prefer understated elegance (shibumi): subdued, elegant use of color and minimal ornamentation and clutter — the original 'less is more'.
Use the suggestive rather than the descriptive or obvious: let words and images together arouse the viewer's imagination instead of spelling every detail out.
Use empty (negative) space deliberately as a design value and eliminate distraction and noise to increase clarity.
Prize the quality of the evidence and experience over the sheer quantity of data or the length of the presentation.
Amplify meaning through simplification: stripping an image or message down to its essential meaning amplifies that meaning.
Reduce text and elements to the essential minimum, removing any word or element that is not strictly needed.
Simplifying a visual means focusing on the essential details, not merely eliminating detail.
A simple visual style does not require simple content; reducing visual complexity need not dumb down the message.
Design is more about subtraction than addition; make conscious decisions about what to include and exclude.
Do not overload slides with details to look smart or well-prepared; information that does not help tell the story forces the audience to hunt for the point and hurts comprehension.
There is no cookie-cutter design; the most appropriate design depends on the content, context, and audience.
Aim for the highest possible signal-to-noise ratio: maximize relevant relative to irrelevant elements, and minimize or remove any element that can go without compromising the message.
Reduce cognitive strain, because people have a limited capacity to process new information efficiently.
Cut visual noise concretely: thin, lighten, or remove grid and table lines, remove footers and logos, and avoid ambiguous labels, icons, or unnecessary emphasis.
Make visual distinctions as subtle as possible while still clear and effective (the smallest effective difference).
The nonessential is not always noise: retain emotional or supportive elements when they serve the message, guided by clarity and balance for the particular audience and objective.
exception: when the element degrades clarity or distracts from the core message

statement: For quantitative displays such as charts and tables, favor the highest signal-to-noise ratio without adornment; a clean data graphic can stand powerfully on its own.
Use 2-D charts for 2-D data and avoid 3-D charts, which add non-data ink, appear less accurate, and make it hard to see where points sit on an axis.
exception: if a 3-D chart must be used, avoid extreme perspectives

statement: Minimize the ratio of ink to data: strip extra ink that does not carry information.
Do not place the company logo on every slide; remove logos from all but the first and last slide to cut clutter.
On-screen clutter measurably reduces viewers' comprehension and retention, so remove it rather than adding more.
Do not present slide after slide of bulleted lists; no one gives a good live presentation that way.
Conventional advice such as the '1-7-7 rule' or five-to-eight lines of bullets is ineffective for a live talk; bullets suit scanning documents, not live presentation.
Use bullet points only rarely, as an exception, after considering more visual options for the information.
condition: a clear bulleted list can be appropriate for summarizing specifications or reviewing process steps

statement: Apply the picture superiority effect: pictures are recalled better than words (notably more than 30 seconds after exposure); pair pictures and words reinforcing the same information, and the effect is strongest for common, concrete things.
Replace descriptive on-screen text with a photograph or appropriate image wherever possible.
exception: text is still needed for labeling and similar functions

statement: Use images as mnemonic devices and use before/after or then-and-now visual comparisons, which are easy to create and easy to remember.
Let images bleed off the edge to fill the whole screen, and ensure text and image work in harmony with enough contrast that the text is not lost.
Invest more of your own preparation time to save the audience's collective time; optimize for the audience's time, not your own convenience.
When premium stock imagery is unaffordable, use low-cost royalty-free micro-stock or free Creative-Commons image sources for professional-quality photos.
Displaying short, legible quotations can be a powerful slide technique; keep quotes short, use them sparingly, and do not read long paragraphs off the screen.
Quotations from credible sources add credibility to your argument and can serve as a springboard into the next topic.
Set a quotation or text within a large full-slide background image rather than beside a small photo, choosing an image with enough empty space and contrast for the text to remain legible.
condition: the background image has ample empty space and provides good contrast with the text

statement: Empty space is not wasted space; it is an active element that gives the remaining elements their power and conveys elegance, clarity, and quality.
Resist the urge to fill empty areas; break a crowded slide into several slides rather than cramming everything onto one.
Avoid 'trapped' space and instead use active empty space to guide the viewer's eyes through the slide.
Use images to guide the viewer's eye toward the most important elements, and when using photos of people ensure their gaze points toward, not away from, the key element.
Give each design one clear, unified message and a clear starting point that guides the viewer; the viewer should never have to think about where to look.
Establish a clear visual hierarchy so the most important, less important, and least important parts of the design are obvious.
Use asymmetrical designs to activate empty space and add dynamic interest, reserving symmetrical designs for a more static, formal, or stable feel, and mix both across a deck.
Treat empty space as a shape you deliberately manipulate; otherwise its use will be accidental and far less powerful.
Build visuals on a clean, simple grid to align elements harmoniously and save time; limiting your choices beats the 'absolute freedom' of positioning every element by hand.
Use the rule of thirds — placing key subjects at the intersection points of a 3x3 grid rather than dead center — as a guideline for balanced, higher-quality visuals.
condition: the rule of thirds is a guideline, not an absolute rule

statement: Apply contrast: make elements that are different clearly and strongly different, not slightly, because contrast creates the focal point and energy and lets the viewer grasp the design quickly, whereas weak contrast is boring and confusing.
Contrast can be achieved through any design element — space, color, type, size, texture, or position — so use whichever fits the message.
Apply repetition: reuse the same or similar elements (color, type, background, a motif) across a deck to create unity, consistency, and cohesion.
exception: avoid over-repeating tired built-in template motifs that become monotonous

statement: Apply alignment: connect every element visually via an invisible line and align each element with another (grids help), because elements that are almost-but-not-quite aligned look unprofessional.
Apply proximity: group related items close together so they read as a unit and keep unrelated items apart, because audiences interpret near items as related and distant items as unrelated.
Do not make the audience work to decipher a slide's organization or priority, such as which caption belongs to which graphic.
A slide is not a page in a book or magazine, so limit it to a few elements or groups of elements.
When self-reviewing a design, step back and notice where your eye is drawn first, second, and so on, to check the intended visual path.
Judge a slide against the basic design principles, but recognize that its true effectiveness can only be assessed when seen used in a live talk.
Aim supportive slides at clarity, not at 'looking good': make them simple, highly visual, and augmenting of the narrative — principled slides end up attractive as a by-product.
For complex content, build or animate a chart or diagram in logical steps rather than revealing it all at once.
Reduce noise by making an image's background match or become transparent to the slide background so image and text blend into a unified, cleaner visual.
Be fully present and mindful during delivery, setting aside other concerns to be with the audience in that moment.
Rehearse and prepare intensively; a presentation that looks effortless is the product of hard practice, not innate talent.
Advance your own slides and effects smoothly without drawing attention to it, keeping the visuals in sync with your words.
Deliver with genuine passion and conviction and do not hold back, because audiences connect with authentic emotion more than with flawless technique.
Continuously observe yourself, the audience, and the environment and adapt, including consciously deciding when to stop or adjust the talk's length.

Respond to hostile or heckling audience members calmly and respectfully without irritation or defensiveness — flowing with it rather than butting heads — and treat them as never the enemy, since most of the audience likely supports you and visible anger loses them.
Focus on making a contribution rather than on impressing people, winning them over, or comparing yourself to others.
Do not dwell on mistakes; reframe a mistake as a learning opportunity and stay present, because you cannot worry about errors and be fully present at the same time.
Treat a presentation as a two-way connection and conversation, not a one-way exhibition, and work to bridge the distance between presenter and audience.
Keep the focus on the audience and the message — it is about them, not about you.
Plan well, but remain flexible and open to the possibilities that arise in the moment.
For a complex or controversial topic, use engaging photographs and easy-to-understand facts so the audience can relate to and visualize the point, rather than dense bar graphs or heady quotes.
Audience concentration drops sharply after about 15 to 20 minutes, so presentation length matters and shorter is generally better.
Never go over your allotted time; aim to finish a little early, around 90 to 95 percent of the time given.
Reject 'more is better' thinking; brevity and clarity beat padding a talk to fill the allotted time.
Leave the audience satisfied but wanting a little more, ending on a high note and favoring quality of material over sheer quantity.
Remove the physical and psychological barriers between you and the audience; avoid presenting from behind a lectern or podium when possible.
exception: a lectern is acceptable at a formal ceremony or when you are one of many speakers taking turns at center stage

statement: Stand front and center so that both you and the screen are the focus; do not sit to the side operating the computer while the audience only watches the screen.
Keep the lights on so the audience can see you, because much of your message is conveyed visually and vocally rather than by words alone.
Find a lighting balance — dim only the front lights if the screen washes out — but never present in the dark.
Use a small, simple wireless remote (advance, back, and blank-screen) and a wireless microphone so you can step away from the computer and move freely to connect with the audience.
Keep the presentation technology as invisible to the audience as possible.
Appeal to both the logical and the emotional: pair solid content and logical structure with a genuine emotional connection.
Improve by actually presenting often; seek out real opportunities to practise speaking and designing visuals.
Develop a critical design eye by studying everyday graphic design around you, such as advertisements, posters, and signage.
There is no quick fix or off-the-shelf panacea for presentation excellence; it is a skill built through study and deliberate practice.
There is no single formula for a great talk; applying one set formula is likely to backfire because audiences detect it and feel manipulated.
Freshness is a core part of a talk's appeal; a talk that feels too similar to one the audience has already heard has less impact.
Treat talk advice as a set of tools to encourage variety, not as rules prescribing one way to speak; use only the tools that fit you and the specific speaking occasion.
A speaker's only real job is to have something valuable to say and to say it authentically in their own voice.
Facility with public speaking is not an innate gift granted to a lucky few; it is a broad set of learnable, teachable skills.
Presentation literacy is a core skill for the twenty-first century, not an optional extra for a few.
Fear of public speaking is near-universal; surveys of top fears often rank it first, ahead of snakes, heights, and even death.
Public-speaking anxiety stems from reputation stakes: humans are social animals and sense that a public performance will affect their standing for better or worse.
With the right mindset a speaker can use fear as an asset, letting it drive proper preparation for the talk.
condition: the speaker adopts the right mindset

statement: Do not try to imitate a famous orator; be yourself — a scientist should present as a scientist, an artist as an artist, rather than faking another style.
You do not need to raise a crowd to its feet with thunderous oratory; conversational sharing can work just as well and for most audiences is better.
exception: a setting that specifically calls for formal oratory

statement: If you can talk to a group of friends over dinner, you already know enough to speak publicly.
Careful preparation combined with speaking from the heart — with openness, conviction, and vulnerability — can make even a technically awkward talk effective.
Rehearsing a talk several times in front of a live audience builds a speaker's confidence to the point where their personality shows through.
Framing a story — finding the right place to begin and building a natural narrative sequence — is essential preparation work for a talk.
A speaker's number-one mission is to take something that matters deeply to them and rebuild it inside the minds of listeners; that something is an idea.
An idea is a mental construct listeners can hold on to, walk away with, value, and be changed by.
A talk succeeds when it plants an idea inside listeners' minds, even if other aspects of the talk are flawed.
Visible nervousness does not necessarily hurt a speaker; it can make them more engaging and endearing to the audience.
Modern technology lets a speaker have outsized impact by talking intimately to a video camera; reaching thousands live is no longer required.
Anyone with an idea worth sharing can give a powerful talk; the one thing that truly matters is having something worth saying, not confidence, stage presence, or smooth talking.

An idea can be anything that changes how people see the world — a simple how-to, a human insight told through story, a meaningful image, a hoped-for future, or a reminder of what matters; it need not be a breakthrough.

People judge poorly whether their own ideas deserve an audience: some overestimate their value while others (often those who undervalue their work) underestimate it, so check your self-assessment with people who know you well.
Style without substance is bad; if the goal is only stage stardom, stop and first develop something genuinely worth sharing.
A speaker's unique first-person experience is valid talk material; many of the best talks are simply a personal story plus a simple lesson drawn from it.
Use the public-speaking commitment as motivation to dive deep and research the topic; you do not need perfect knowledge today, only the incentive to discover it.

The questions asked during research — what matters most, how issues relate, what is hard to explain, what riddles lack answers, what the key controversies are — can supply the blueprint and key revelation moments of the talk.
If, after genuine effort to find something worth saying, you are still floundering, it is acceptable and sometimes better to decline the invitation to speak.
condition: genuine effort to find a worthwhile idea has failed

statement: Language re-creates an idea in a listener's mind only to the extent the underlying concepts are shared by speaker and listener; you can only use tools the audience already has access to.
Start from the audience's language, concepts, assumptions, and values (their common ground), not your own; starting only from yours will fail.
Plain shared language conjures vivid mental images that precise technical or jargon-laden phrasing of the same request fails to produce.

Language alone can conjure in a listener's brain the same mental patterns that direct experience produces, as shown by fMRI evidence that listeners' brain patterns matched those of people who had watched the original film.

The claim that only 7 percent of communication is verbal (Mehrabian's 7/38/55) is a misapplication; his study concerned how emotion is communicated, not communication overall, so do not use it to downplay words.

Tone of voice and body language matter greatly for conveying emotion, but the substance of a talk — telling a story, building an idea, explaining, arguing, or calling to action — depends crucially on the words.
Treat a talk as a journey speaker and audience take together: like a tour guide, begin where the audience is and allow no impossible leaps or unexplained shifts in direction.
Focusing on what you will give the audience is the ideal foundation for preparing a talk.
The speaker's job is to give to the audience, not take from them; audiences sense a selling agenda quickly and disengage, so avoid turning a talk into a sales pitch.
exception: you were specifically invited to present the product, book, or organization

statement: Generosity in a talk evokes a response: giving value without asking can yield more than pitching would, as when a speaker who made no appeal still drew contributions exceeding his need.
Do not ramble or wing it, and never boast about being underprepared; the audience gives irrecoverable time and attention, and wasting it insults them — preparation is mandatory.

Do not frame a talk around your organization's history, structure, or products (the Org Bore); focus on the nature of the work and the power of its ideas, anchoring to discoveries and insights rather than organizational acts.

Inspiration cannot be performed or faked; it must be earned and is an audience response to authenticity, courage, selfless work, and genuine wisdom, so pursuing applause or charisma directly backfires and reads as manipulation.
Style-over-substance talks harm the whole genre by making audiences less receptive when a genuinely inspiring speaker follows.
The number-one reason talks fail to say something meaningful is that the speaker never planned the talk as a whole, working point-by-point without spending time on the overall arc.
Every talk should have a throughline: the connecting theme onto which every narrative element is attached.
A throughline does not restrict a talk to one topic, story, or direction; it only requires that all the pieces connect.
Encapsulate the throughline in no more than fifteen words that carry robust content — the precise idea and takeaway, not a vague goal like 'I want to inspire the audience.'
A throughline should have an unexpected or intriguing angle; avoid predictable, banal framings such as 'the importance of hard work.'
Present just one idea as thoroughly and completely as the time allows; decide what you want the audience to understand unambiguously by the end.
Choose a single big idea larger than you or your organization, but leverage your own experience to show it is not empty speculation.
A throughline is not the same as a topic; even a clearly assigned topic admits several possible throughlines, so the speaker must still choose one.

The first step in finding a throughline is to learn as much as possible about the audience — who they are, their knowledge, expectations, and concerns — because you can only gift an idea to minds ready to receive that type of idea.
The TED talk length limit is 18 minutes: short enough to hold attention (including online) yet long enough to say something that matters.
A shorter talk requires more preparation time, not less.
Condensing by cramming every topic into summary form fails: overstuffed equals underexplained, and rushed multi-topic material does not land with the audience.
To say something interesting, take the time to show why it matters (the question, problem, or experience) and to flesh out each point with real examples, stories, and facts.
The right way to fit a time limit is to slash the range of topics down to a single connected thread that can be properly developed; you cover less but achieve significantly greater impact.
The secret of successful talks often lies in what is left out; be prepared to 'kill your darlings' and cut material you love that is not part of the main narrative.
Plan the talk, then cut it by half, then cut it another 50 percent; ask what you can unpack meaningfully in the time, not how much you can fit in.
A talk built around a single vivid moment is more interesting and revealing than a comprehensive summary of many facts.
Regardless of the time limit, you will only cover as much ground as you can dive into in sufficient depth to be compelling.

Build a structure in which every element links back to the throughline; many structures work (tree, connected loop, What/So-What/Now-What), so choose the one that most powerfully develops your throughline in the available time.

For a heavy or distressing subject, frame the talk as an idea (leads with curiosity, proposes a solution, 'isn't this interesting?') rather than an issue (leads with morality, exposes a problem, 'isn't this terrible?'), because relentless issue-talks cause compassion fatigue and audiences switch off.
exception: you are confident the listeners are ready and willing to be made uncomfortable

statement: Test your throughline out loud on someone who could be a typical audience member; saying it verbally crystallizes what is clear, what is missing, and how to sharpen it.
Prepare the talk for an audience of one — a specific intelligent, curious person you like, not a demographic — which brings warmth of spirit to the delivery.
Pick a topic that lives deep within you and that you know and love; a well-worn passion captivates more than a fresh gimmick chosen for novelty.

Vet the throughline against key questions before committing: is it fresh rather than already out there, can it truly be explained in the time slot with necessary examples, do you know enough and have the credibility, and is it a gift rather than an ask?
Knowledge cannot be pushed into a brain; it must be pulled in, so before building an idea you need the audience's permission.
Impact requires a human connection first; without it, even brilliant content with clear explanations and sharp logic will not land and is merely filed away and forgotten.

Audiences carry defensive weapons — skepticism, mistrust, dislike, boredom, incomprehension — that evaluate incoming ideas, so the speaker's first job is to disarm them and build a trusting human bond.
Make eye contact right from the start: walk on confidently, look around, meet the eyes of two or three people, and smile before beginning.
Humans form instant judgments from very light cues, and a genuine natural smile is the best single tool to engender the trust that lets minds sync.
Sustained eye contact between two people triggers mirror-neuron activity that adopts the other's emotional state, so a speaker's calm or nerves transfer to the audience.
A smile must be genuine: people detect fake smiles and immediately feel manipulated.
condition: the smile is authentic rather than performed

statement: Do not rush the opening sentence; walk into the light, pick out a couple of people, meet their eyes, nod a greeting, and smile first.
Revealing your own vulnerability early is one of the best ways to disarm an audience, signaling you carry no threat so they relax.
Nervousness can work in a speaker's favor: audiences sense it and root for the speaker rather than despising them, so be ready to acknowledge it plainly if needed.
Vulnerability requires boundaries — vulnerability minus boundaries is not vulnerability but oversharing — and formulaic or contrived personal sharing leaves audiences feeling manipulated and hostile.

Only share personal material you have already worked through: a story is ready to share only when your healing and growth do not depend on the audience's response, and the sharing serves the work on stage rather than your own processing.
condition: you have owned the story and no longer need the audience's reaction to heal

statement: Humor builds connection and social bonding; audiences who laugh with you come to like you and are then far readier to take your message seriously, because laughter blows open their defenses.
Early laughter is a signal of connection — to the speaker (nerves ease) and to the whole room (the group has bonded with the speaker) — after which everyone pays more attention.
Prefer hilarious-but-true stories relevant to your topic, or an endearing humorous use of language, over canned jokes; jokes per se seem hackneyed and a downloaded joke will probably backfire.
Ineffective humor is worse than no humor at all; if you are not funny, do not try to be — test any humor on friends or colleagues and cut it if they do not laugh.
condition: you are unsure the humor works

statement: Avoid humor based on gender, race, disability, religion, ethnicity, or politics, along with off-color remarks, puns, sarcasm, and limericks; outsiders to a community especially cannot joke about it, and offense is hard to recover from.
Keep a funny remark ready for when you flub your words or the A/V fails; the audience has been there and will instantly give you their sympathy.
Timing is critical for humor: give a laughter moment the chance to land by pausing, without appearing to fish for applause.
Avoid imitating accents other than your own unless you are extremely talented, as it usually reads as embarrassing on a public stage.
Park your ego: nothing damages a talk more than the sense that the speaker is a blowhard, so even if you have real accomplishments, let the audience discover them for themselves.
Be yourself; the worst talks come from people trying to be someone they are not.
exception: the real you is arrogant and self-centered, in which case adopt a more generous persona

statement: Self-deprecation in the right hands wins laughter, affection, and trust, and can defuse a potentially hostile audience.
Ego leaks in ways invisible to a speaker used to attention — name-dropping, show-off stories, boasting about achievements, and making the talk about you rather than a usable idea.
Because self-importance is hard to see from the inside, try the talk on a trusted person who will honestly tell you if you come across as full of yourself.
Stories build connection as instant generators of interest, empathy, and emotion, and can be used to open a talk, to illustrate in the middle, or (less often) to close.

The stories that generate the best connection are about you personally or people close to you — authentic tales of failure, awkwardness, misfortune, or danger — which shift listeners from mild interest to deep engagement.

Beware stories that read as boastful or emotionally manipulative, such as a self-glorifying problem-to-triumph arc or a last-minute tragic reveal, which can make an audience uncomfortable rather than sympathetic.
The overriding guideline for connection is authenticity: test a story by whether you would tell it to a group of old friends, because audiences, like friends, detect the inauthentic.
Connection techniques must not come across as techniques; they have to be part of a genuine desire to connect, treating listeners as fellow humans and friends.
Tribal thinking around politics, religion, or race is the biggest killer of connection: a community that has wholesale rejected your ideas will shut down and stop listening when it feels threatened.
Partisan or tribal identity can block a message regardless of its merit, as when half an audience refused to accept a climate case purely because a politician from the opposing side made it.

To reach people who radically disagree with you, put yourself in their shoes, avoid language that triggers tribal responses, start from the world as seen through their eyes, and build connection on shared humanity.
condition: the audience holds views strongly opposed to your thesis

statement: The human mind coevolved with storytelling, so stories are easy to follow via their simple linear structure and everyone can relate to them, unlike complex explanations or arguments.
Listeners empathize with a story's characters and physically feel what the characters feel, which holds attention and makes them care about the outcome.
The classic story formula is: a protagonist with goals meets an unexpected obstacle, a crisis results, the protagonist attempts to overcome it leading to a climax, and finally a denouement.

When telling a story from the stage, emphasize four things: base it on a character the audience can empathize with, build tension, offer the right level of detail (neither too little nor too much), and end with a satisfying resolution.

Know why you are telling a story and edit out every detail not needed to make your point, while leaving enough for listeners to vividly imagine what happened; overstuffing with personally important but irrelevant detail, or omitting essential context, ruins a story.
Do not reveal a story's key intent or twist too early, because doing so kills the drama and the audience's emotional experience.

A talk built around a single story hands the speaker major benefits: the narrative arc supplies the throughline, it evokes an intense audience response, a personal story creates empathy, and the linear structure is easy to remember — making it the simplest talk to prepare.

A personal story does not automatically give the audience a takeaway; without a central idea that wraps the narrative together it is a missed opportunity, and this is one of the biggest reasons speaking applications are turned down.

Artfully edit your personal journey to link its critical moments so that others can derive meaning, and reveal each step with humility, honesty, and vulnerability rather than as self-indulgent rambling.
A personal story must be true; exaggerating or fabricating is the easiest way to destroy your reputation, because once a talk is public a single viewer noticing the falsehood can undo you.

Draw meaning out of a story without force-feeding the exact conclusion (which insults the audience), but ensure there is enough for listeners to connect the dots; a metaphorical story (parable) needs much greater elucidation for an audience outside your field than for insiders.
condition: the audience is outside your field

statement: A parable can entertain, inform, and inspire at once, but carries real risks: the analogy may not fit and can mislead, or you may spend so long on the story that you fail to draw out the conclusions.
Begin an explanation right where the audience already is, both literally and conceptually, without daunting assumptions about their prior knowledge.
Light a fire of curiosity early: the sense that something does not quite make sense — a knowledge gap that must be closed — is what opens a mind and makes it want new ideas.
Introduce the concepts an explanation depends on one at a time, because understanding is built as a hierarchy in which each layer supplies the elements that construct the next.
Use metaphors and analogies to connect puzzling new facts to the audience's existing mental model; they reveal the shape of a new concept so the mind knows how to slot it into place.
Use examples and little stories to lock an explanation into place, letting the listener test whether the new idea actually fits the facts.
Plan the balance between the concepts you introduce and the examples and metaphors needed to make them understandable; without that shaping the concepts cannot be put in place.

Explanation is the act of consciously adding a new element to someone's mental model or reordering existing elements more satisfyingly, and it is the essential tool for building an idea inside a mind.
Presenting baffling or unexpected facts opens a knowledge gap that makes the mind crave resolution, which a speaker can use to drive an explanation forward.
Giving a concept a name makes an otherwise slippery mystery more believable and easier for the audience to hold on to.

To explain a powerful new idea, ask what the audience already knows, what the connecting theme is, which concepts are necessary to build the explanation, and what metaphors and examples will reveal those concepts.

The curse of knowledge is a cognitive bias in which we cannot remember what it feels like not to know something we know well; overcoming it may be the single most important requirement for communicating clearly.

Being merely conscious of the curse of knowledge is not enough: share a draft with friends and colleagues, beg for ruthless feedback on anything unclear, then test it on a private audience and explicitly ask 'Did that make sense? Was anything confusing?'
Recruit help specifically from people new to the topic, because they are best at spotting the gaps a knowledgeable speaker cannot see.

Long-term memory depends on coherent hierarchical organization (chunks within chunks), so a speaker's challenge is to convey that multidimensional structure through the one-dimensional, one-word-after-another medium of speech.

Make explicit how each sentence relates logically to the one before it — similarity, contrast, elaboration, cause, effect, or violated expectation — and signal whether a point is a digression, the main argument, or an exception, using structural signpost phrases.

The listener must always know where she is on the talk's tree of throughline and branches; the curse of knowledge strikes hardest when every sentence is understandable but the speaker forgets to show how they link.
Sequence sentences and concepts precisely so that understanding builds naturally, reordering material when a listener reports the link is unclear.
Do a jargon check: eliminate or explain any technical terms and acronyms unfamiliar to your listeners, because when jargon piles up the audience simply switches off.

Make everything as simple as it can be but no simpler: do not over-explain or spell out what the audience already knows, since some specialist terms are essential and over-simplifying insults their intelligence.

The best explainers say just enough to let the audience feel they are arriving at the idea themselves — describing a concept's shape just enough for prepared minds to snap it into place — which is efficient for the speaker and deeply satisfying for listeners.
Before building your idea, make clear what it is not: ruling out plausible alternatives shrinks the space of possibilities so the audience can close in on exactly what you mean.
A well-built explanation can generate real excitement; make the topic personally relevant to the audience first, then stir curiosity with an unexpected question before building the concept.

Persuasion requires demolition before construction: you must convince the audience that their current view of the world is not quite right, taking down the parts that do not work before rebuilding something better.
Minds must be primed before they can be persuaded, so prime the audience in several different ways before reaching the main argument.

Priming uses intuition pumps — metaphors, stories, or linguistic devices that intuitively make a conclusion seem more plausible; this is not rigorous argument but a way of nudging the audience in your direction.
Present statistics relative to the right denominator, such as population size, rather than as raw totals, because what matters to the audience is individual probability, not the aggregate count.

Reason delivers conclusions at a higher level of certainty than any other mental tool and, once accepted, lodges permanently; but it must be broken into small steps that are each totally convincing and that start from something the audience already sees to be true, driven by an if-then mechanism.

Reductio ad absurdum strengthens a position by taking the opposing view and showing it leads to a contradiction; speakers commonly tap its spirit by offering a dramatic counterexample that is self-evidently ridiculous.
Undercutting the credibility of the opposing position is powerful but must be handled with care: aim it at issues rather than directly at opponents, or it drifts from reason into mudslinging.
condition: the attack targets an argument, not a person

statement: The detective-story structure starts with a big mystery, then travels through candidate solutions ruling them out one by one until only one survives, so that the audience feels it took the learning journey and persuades itself.

The detective structure works because it taps our love of stories while carrying an underlying logic — if every alternative is false and only one viable option remains, that option must be true — turning daunting subjects into intriguing ones.

Watertight logic is necessary but not sufficient for persuasion: people can be convinced by logic yet not energized by it, so reason must be bolstered by tools that make the conclusion meaningful, exciting, and desirable.
Inject humor early in a demanding reason-based talk to signal that the hard thinking ahead will also be enjoyable.
Add an anecdote that reveals how you became engaged with the issue; it humanizes you, and once people know why you are passionate they are more likely to follow your logic.
Offer vivid examples, such as a dramatic optical illusion, to make an abstract claim concrete and felt rather than merely asserted.
Recruiting third-party validation can make an argument more persuasive, but handle it carefully because such an appeal is not itself a valid argument and its effect depends on the audience.
condition: the audience gives weight to the cited authority

statement: Use powerful visuals, such as proportional charts that change on screen as you speak, to make a persuasive point land with impact.
Reason is the best tool for building wisdom over the long term: a robust argument gathers adherents gradually even when not immediately accepted, like a slow-growing oak whose roots run deep.
The most direct way to gift an idea is to show it: in a revelation talk you reveal your work — images, a demo, or a vision — in a way that delights and inspires.

A revelation talk's success depends on what is being revealed, so match your goal to the type: aesthetic wonder for images, amazement and new possibility for a demo, a vivid desirable future for a vision.

A wonder walk reveals a succession of images or wonder moments one simple step at a time, and works best when a clear linking theme or throughline pulls the pieces together rather than flat 'now my next project' transitions.
When revealing visual work, provide context that dials up the sense of wonder, not merely describes what is on screen.

Describe creative work in accessible human language: obscure, over-intellectualized metaconcepts (paradigm, dialectic, framework, approach) are worse than technical jargon and destroy comprehension when they pile up, so use them sparingly.
Lift the lid on your creative process — share what you were dreaming of, the mistakes, and the dead ends — because revealing the process is one of the key gifts of any creative talk.
For visual work, cut the number of words way back and let the visuals carry the talk (a 12-minute talk can reveal over 100 images), and use silence as a rarely-used tool to amplify their power.
Automatically advancing, pre-timed slides can keep a visual walk energetic and enforce a dynamic pace.

Business presentations improve when reframed as wonder walks: link the projects to build excitement, pair each step with an intriguing image, and switch the tone from 'look what we've achieved' to 'look how intriguing this is.'
When revealing a technology, invention, or new process, do not just look at it — demonstrate it working, since a great live demo can be the most memorable part of a conference.
The single most important factor in a demo talk is the quality of whatever you are demonstrating.
Do not spend the first half of a demo talk on complicated context before the audience has seen the thing in action, or they will switch off; give an intriguing tease first.
A reliable demo structure is: an initial tease, then the necessary background and invention story, then the demo itself (as visual and dramatic as possible), then the implications of the technology.
exception: never fake the demonstration

statement: Showing beats telling: turning theory into a live physical proof wins an audience over more powerfully than explaining it.

Painting a compelling picture of the future — the world not as it is but as it might be — is one of the greatest gifts a speaker can bring, making an audience's minds explode with a sense of possibility.
There are two keys to sharing a dream effectively: paint a bold picture of the alternative future you desire, and do it in a way that makes others desire that future too.
Painting a future vision often requires visual aids, because revealing speculative ideas visually makes them seem far more convincing than describing them in words.

When a future vision could unsettle an audience, make clear why that future is worth pursuing and frame it around human values rather than clever technology alone; humor and a concrete, actionable path both reduce the discomfort.
condition: the technology or vision could seem creepy or alarming

statement: The talk-building techniques (connection, narration, explanation, persuasion, revelation) are tools rather than limits, and most talks mix several, so select, mix, match, and augment them for the idea you wish to build.

Before adding slides, ask whether you need them at all: at least a third of the most-viewed TED talks use none, and slides pull attention from the speaker to the screen, which can undercut a talk whose power is personal connection.
condition: the core of the talk is intensely personal

statement: For every speaker, having no slides at all is better than having bad slides.
For a revelation image, set the context and prime the audience first, then reveal it full-screen with minimal adornment so the visual works its magic.
Limit each slide to a single core idea; since extra slides now cost nothing, replace one overly complex slide with several simple slides you click through in the same time.
A talk and its slides run as two parallel cognitive streams, so design where the audience's attention goes and ensure a high-cognitive-load slide does not fight with what you are saying.
When you have finished talking about an image, cut to a blank black slide so the audience takes a break from visuals and refocuses on your words.

Highlight the exact point a graph or chart is making (for example, coloring the relevant elements), and use separate builds or slides for separate comparisons rather than cramming them onto one slide.
Do not put your spoken words on slides: text-and-bullet decks are the surest way to lose an audience, because they read ahead and your points feel stale by the time you reach them.
A text slide should tease the audience's curiosity with a question rather than state the answer, then deliver the information in spoken form, which makes your words more interesting rather than less.
The purpose of visuals is to share what your mouth cannot do well — photographs, video, animation, and key data — not to duplicate the words you are already speaking.
Show images generously: concepts in a talk must be limited but images need not be, you do not have to explain every image, and even a five-second silent view can have impact.

Build slides from a blank template rather than the software's built-in bullet templates, and for photographs use a black background and show them full-bleed at the highest available resolution to avoid pixelation on large screens.

Use a single medium-weight sans-serif typeface at 24 points or larger, with at most three sizes that each serve a purpose, and choose font colors for high contrast, never light-on-light or dark-on-dark.
Avoid bullets, dashes, underlining, italics, and multiple type effects on a slide (bold is acceptable), and verify legibility by viewing the slides from six to twelve feet on the actual display.

Reveal complex slides with builds that add one element per click and give time to absorb each step, and keep video clips short (rarely over 30 seconds, only a few per talk) using your own authentic, high-production footage.
Avoid gimmicky slide transitions; use only cut or dissolve so that the transition never calls attention to itself.
Secure a legal license for all photos, video, music, and fonts, or use your own work, Creative Commons, or outright-free assets.

Test a presentation two ways: on non-expert friends (asking what they understood, did not understand, and still wonder), and technically on the actual equipment — never present without walking through slides and videos on the gear that will be used.
Keep photo credits and attributions consistent, small, and unobtrusive so they do not pull the audience's focus from the images.
There is no single right way to deliver a talk, and forcing a scripted, memorized approach on a speaker whose natural style is fluent in-the-moment explanation can make the talk implode.

What matters most in delivery is that the speaker is comfortable and confident, giving the talk in the mode that best lets them focus on their passion, so adapt the format (even a lectern with notes) to the speaker.
Decide early whether you will write the talk out as a full script to be read or memorized, or instead work out a clear structure and speak in the moment to each point.
Speaking without a lectern and from the heart is human-to-human communication in its purest form and audiences respond to that vulnerability.
Variety in delivery has power: at a multi-day event the speakers who stand out are often those who do things differently from everyone else.
McCandless-style reframing shows a single well-chosen alternative view of the same data (such as a metric normalized differently) can sharpen the audience's worldview dramatically.
Include at most one photo of yourself in your working environment unless more are needed to tell the story, and avoid yearbook-style team photos, which matter to you but not to the audience.

Scripting a talk lets you make the best use of limited time by tweaking every sentence to perfection, and lets drafts be shared ahead for feedback; it is especially valuable when tricky explanations or precise persuasion steps are involved.

Being read to and being spoken to are very different experiences, and audiences respond far more powerfully to being spoken to, because watching someone think out loud in real time conveys conviction that gives listeners permission to embrace the meaning.
